Last evening when the house rose I was endeavouring to point out to the minister the need for having some form of coastguard protection on the great lakes. At that time I pointed out that no facilities for rescue work were immediately available and that in emergencies, as I understand it, the R.C.A.F. could be called upon to assist and, on certain occasions, the Ontario provincial police.
I should like to say that I think these methods or procedures are not at all suitable or not at all what is needed to provide this necessary service. While some form of coastguard service on the great lakes is necessary during all 12 months of the year, nevertheless the need for a coastguard service is greatest during the months of June, July, August and September. During the other months of the year there are fishing boats on the lakes and some pleasure craft, but it is during those four summer months that the greatest need for a coastguard service presents itself.
As I mentioned yesterday, hardly a day passes that you do not read in one of the newspapers of some unfortunate occurrence on the great lakes. I have a great many clippings in this regard but I see no point in wasting the time of the committee by reading them because every hon. member knows as well as I do that these conditions exist.
There has been some editorial comment in this respect. I should like to refer briefly to parts of an editorial from the Tillsonburg News of March 31 last, the Tillsonburg News being a large weekly newspaper in Ontario. I refer to only parts of the editorial but I think they cogently express the views of the public generally in that part of the province. Under the heading "Rescue Service Needed on Lakes" we find this comment:
We have seen tragedy strike along the lake-front. It is only through good fortune that the loss of life was not greater.
This editorial refers specifically to an extremely unfortunate incident on lake Erie this spring. The editorial continues:
This is not the first time disaster has struck on the great lakes, and it will not be the last.
The great lakes provide the livelihood for thousands in the fishing and transportation industries and are the playgrounds for countless thousands 50433-411
Supply-Transport	'
more. Boats-from rowboats and small outboard craft to the giant grain, ore and oil carriers-dot the lakes from spring break-up to winter freeze-up.
What protection is there for the thousands at work and play?
Then I continue reading further down in the editorial:
As a minimum provision there should be adequate lifeboats and other rescue equipment at each port and trained volunteer crews to operate this equipment, and an adequate storm warning service for all small craft using the lakes. When disaster strikes there should be no need to wait for equipment to be brought long distances to effect a rescue. Time can mean life and death.
The editorial has a great deal more to say but I do not intend to refer to any more of it. The need for a coastguard service on the great lakes has existed for some time but the conditions have been aggravated since the end of world war II. With the increase in population in the southern part of Ontario and with the great increase in the real wealth of people, people who live inland, people who work in factories now have boats available on the lakes for their week-end pleasure. On lake Erie alone in one small area involving Port Dover, Long Point and Turkey Point there are literally several thousand small boats. I have no idea what number of boats there must be on lake Ontario in the Toronto and Hamilton areas, but I presume there must be many more there.
These people go to the lakes for the week ends. Most of them have little experience in navigation. They go out and no one knows where they go, how long they are out or whether they are still out until, as I said yesterday, somebody sees a smoke signal of some kind away out on the lake and people have to be rescued. This sort of thing goes on on lake Erie, lake Ontario and lake Huron. The United States has a very excellent coastguard service. I could go into that at some length but I do not feel it is necessary. I should like to suggest to the minister that he take into consideration some sort of scheme to provide a coastguard service on the great lakes, particularly during the summer months. I point out that it is lake Erie, lake Ontario and lake Huron that are most affected because on those three lakes you find the great majority of pleasure craft. Lake Superior might be considered at another time, but if to start with some sort of service were provided on lakes Erie, Ontario and Huron, it would be very helpful.
I realize that a year-round project on the scale of the United States coastguard system would be very expensive. I suggest that if some type of volunteer rescue service were available at the important fishing ports on

Supply-Transport
lake Erie and lake Huron during the winter months this might provide the service needed at the moment, but during the summer months something much more extensive will have to be arranged. I suggest that at every port of any size on the three lakes I have mentioned there should, during the summer months, be some official who can be contacted if rescue work seems necessary. It might be possible for the federal government to make some arrangement with a provincial body such as the Ontario provincial police to take care of these duties. It might be that some such arrangement could be made which would save money. I think that would be quite possible.
As I have said, first of all you have to have someone to contact if a disaster or an emergency takes place, someone who has the authority to act and can do something immediately because, as was pointed out, time may mean life or death. In the second place, I think a meteorological service should be provided at all ports where pleasure and fishing craft are in evidence along the great lakes. The government has a very excellent meteorological service and there is no reason why it could not be made available to these ports. Again, if it were felt that it would be too expensive and not practical to have someone at each of these ports during the summer months I suggest that the Department of Transport might very well make arrangements with some provincial authority. They could give them some sort of subsidy and make some arrangement. I feel there is no reason why that could not be done.
The third thing that is necessary is that some person with some authority be at these lake ports to check when small boats go out in the lake and when they come in. In a minute I am going to point out how I think this could be done on a fairly economical basis. In this regard I should like to suggest that college students, who are on holidays during the summer, be employed for this purpose. Particularly, I should like to suggest that the university naval training division could be employed on the great lakes in coastguard service as part of their naval training. These people are free during the dangerous summer months and could check on small boats going out of the harbour and could check when they came in in order to make sure some boat was not out all night on the lake.
This type of service could also perform another function. If meteorological reports were received indicating that a storm was likely to occur within the next few hours these people could either warn small boats not to go out on the lake or they could be

given authority to turn them back as the United States coastguard does. If you go to leave any of the harbours on lake Erie, such as Cleveland or Erie, and bad weather is threatening, the coastguard will not let you go out. Of course, there is no such provision on this side. I point out to the minister that I believe this could be done on an economical basis by getting the Minister of National Defence to co-operate with the Minister of Transport to work out some scheme whereby the university naval training division could do this work. If that could not be worked out, we could employ college students for these duties. All they would have to do would be to receive meteorological reports and if bad weather threatened they would turn back the boat. The other thing they would have to do would be to check the boats that go out in the daytime and ascertain whether or not they all came back at night. This is only necessary during the months of June, July, August and September. The principal thing, if nothing else is done, is to have some authority with which people could communicate in case rescue work is necessary, some authority that could act right away to get in touch with the R.C.A.F. or some boat operated by the Department of Transport or arranged for by the department with the Ontario provincial police.
There is no authority in this respect and some very unfortunate accidents have occurred. I refer to one that occurred a year ago when all those boy scouts were drowned in lake Ontario. A few weeks ago two people from my home town were out on lake Erie all night and it was only good fortune that someone picked them up. You only need to refer to the daily newspapers to see that this sort of thing happens frequently. According to the newspapers the last big holiday week end indicated that drowning has surpassed the automobile as the big killer on holiday week ends in Ontario. Not all of these drownings occur because of a lack of coastguard facilities, I am quite prepared to admit that; but a great many have. Again I should like to recommend to the minister that something be done, if not this year at least for next summer.
I do not think it would take much money or much organization.
As a final suggestion in this regard, I would say that on the great lakes there are some very large fishing fleets, particularly at Port Dover. The other ports have them too. These diesel tugs are operated by captains who know the waters inside and out. Most of these ships now have ship to shore telephones. During July and August, the gill net industry on the great lakes is not too

busy. I have had some experience with it and I know that during July and August the catches are not large. It is quite possible that the government could make arrangements with the fish companies to use these boats on alternate days as duty boats to effect rescue work. In Port Dover, which I use as an example, there are about 30 or 35 of these diesel tugs whose captains know the waters very well, that have ship to shore telephones. I would not be surprised if some arrangements could be worked out whereby these tugs could be operated as duty tugs to act in rescue work. Perhaps as an alternative some small boats could be purchased cheaply by the department to do this work.
I do not wish to take up further the time of the committee. However, this is a matter of very considerable concern not only to those people who live in the lake ports located in the counties bordering the lakes, but also to those who live in the inland counties. I know that my own constituency is entirely inland, in southern Ontario, but there are many people who during the summer months go out in boats on the lakes, on excursions and the like. I think there should be some protection for these people in southern Ontario, who form so large a proportion of the population of this country. Perhaps in the old days they did not have small boats, and this may not have been necessary 25 years ago; but it certainly is necessary today.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly on this item. Through the Minister of Transport I would take this opportunity to bring a subject to the attention of the board of transport commissioners for immediate consideration. This matter has been discussed before, and 1 take pleasure in presenting it again, because it concerns the subway of the Canadian Pacific Railway on highway No. 2 at a point just east of Newcastle, Ontario. I am sure many hon. members are familiar with this subway, and probably know it better as the hole in the wall.
In my memory and experience as a newspaperman in that particular area, there have been many serious fatal accidents at this particular point. The main cause of these vehicular crashes is the fact that the subway is narrow and low. As a result, trucks and large transports are forced to take to the centre of the road to get through the subway. Because of this, either the on-coming vehicle is forced to stop to be assured that the road ahead is clear before proceeding through, or it is forced off the road. As a 50433-411J
Supply-Transport
result there have been crashes both from on-coming vehicles and from the rear as well.
Just recently there was a very serious crash at this point and, to bring it to the attention of hon. members and, in particular, that of the board of transport commissioners,
I should like to place on record some comments which appeared in the Port Hope Evening Guide of Saturday, July 16, the day following a recent accident, when it said:
Yesterday this newspaper reported an accident, which from all accounts was directly due to this bottle-neck. A transport stopped to allow another to pass through the "hole-in-the-wall." A Colonial Coach Lines bus carrying 24 passengers crashed into the rear of the transport and 23 people were sent to hospital for treatment. Some were quite seriously injured. From all evidence at hand it is to be assumed the "hole-in-the-wall" was directly responsible for this accident, since otherwise the transport would not have stopped where it did. It was only a miracle that lives were not lost.
This is but one more in a long series of minor and major accidents at this particular point. On several occasions I have mentioned this during sittings of the railway committee, and most recently it was brought up during the discussion of the bill to increase the federal contribution toward eliminating dangerous grade crossings and subways. In addition to my presentations in the matter, both my own newspaper, the Canadian Statesman of Bowmanville, and the Evening Guide of Port Hope on several occasions have urged that corrective action be instituted. Apparently up to date no action has been taken either by the railway, the highways department or the board of transport commissioners.
At this time, in the interests of public safety in that area I would ask again that the board of transport commissioners take independent action without waiting further for the other parties concerned to act. This is an exceptionally dangerous subway on a heavily travelled highway, and it should be eliminated at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Chairman, I have neither a railway nor even a bridge for which to thank the minister. I rise really for the purpose of asking two or three questions in advance. My reason for doing this is that I have had great difficulty in making the minister understand my questions. When I asked him particularly about the Port aux Basques incident he said he could not understand my question. I felt rather chagrined about this, but with the explanation the minister has given I have blamed myself less because it appears quite possible that the minister did not want to understand my questions because he did not have any answers to make to them. At the moment I wish to draw to his attention two or three points

Supply-Transport
on which I want answers at some length. If he does not understand my questions this morning I would be very glad to go around privately and explain them. It is for that reason that I give them in advance because of my misfortunes in the past.
The first thing I would like to ask about is the item covering a director of economic policy and I should like to know whether there is a special economic policy in the Department of Transport. We have been told that there are conflicting economic policies in various departments. For example, we have been told that there was a conflict between the Department of Finance and the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with pipe lines. Of course there are plenty of economists in other departments such as agriculture and defence production; there is a whole list of them where there would be infinite possibilities of different economic policies. So I should like the minister to explain to us the special economic policy of the Department of Transport. That is my first question and I hope I have made it clear because I should like very much to have an answer.
My second question relates to the West Indies steamship lines. It seemed to me in attending the meetings of the committee dealing with publicly owned railway lines, etc., that the attitude toward the West Indies line was always one of hesitation, was rather lukewarm. I could not make up my mind whether it was intended to go all out to make this line a success or whether it was felt it was a fizzle and should be allowed to peter out. That was the impression I gained in the committee. I would be glad if the minister could say something about that, as to the real attitude of the government. I am not suggesting that it is an easy question but our trade relations with the West Indies are important and will become more important and therefore I would be glad if the minister would say something on this point.
The third and last question which I wish to ask the minister-I hope they are getting clearer and clearer as I go on-is with regard to a remark made the other evening by the Minister of Public Works when he was asked about ports on the St. Lawrence seaway. A question was asked about the great inland port of Toronto and at that time the Minister of Public Works replied, as reported on page 6421 of Hansard of July 19, as follows:
This seaway development has precipitated a great many requests from virtually every port along the great lakes to have an investigation carried out to determine what must be undertaken to accommodate deep-sea shipping. It will take some time 
for this whole matter to crystallize to determine which ports will become key ports in the operation. That field of activity falls more appropriately under the Department of Transport, because it does relate to shipping.
This is not the only instance in which the Minister of Public Works has been good enough to refer things to the Minister of Transport, and I refer this also hoping that the minister will speak at some length on this important matter.

Mr. Chairman, on this first item I should like to make reference to something which was touched on very casually by the minister in his remarks yesterday. I should like to impress upon the minister the urgency, indeed the imperative need of undertaking at the earliest possible time the construction of a new airport for the city of Edmonton. I am sure that the minister is aware of the situation in connection with the airport at Edmonton since the problem there is of long standing. Negotiations have been going on for a long time and I may say frankly that the people are disappointed with the delay in the government implementing its pledge that a major airport would be constructed there at an early date.
I have every confidence that the minister is anxious to correct whatever shortcomings there may be in his department and it is for that reason that I wish to draw to his attention certain facts which have been treated indifferently far too long with the result that the people in my home community have been receiving well-publicized statements but very little action. They have been told that the government was on the verge of commencing the construction of a new airport outside Edmonton. They were pleased to hear those reports and were prepared to give every co-operation in the building of such an airport, but all they have received thus far is suspense. I am sure that the minister will agree that that is something which it is difficult to take indefinitely.
I refer of course to the official statement made jointly last year by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys as well as the Minister of Transport that a new airport built to international standards would be constructed for this city. During the course of the present session, I made several inquiries of the minister in order to ascertain just what progress was being made in that regard and the fact that the minister has been unable to announce any commencement date for the construction has added to the

dissatisfaction of the people back home and to their belief that there is stalling at the federal level.
I am sure the minister knows quite well why an airport should be built outside that city. It involves public safety, sound economics and public necessity. Some five years ago the city authorities made representations to the department for the relocation of the airport facilities. It should be remembered that the municipal airport at Edmonton was the first municipal airport licensed in Canada. At that particular time the airport was located on the fringes of the city, but with the expansion which has taken place in that area'

Edmonton is one of the fastest growing cities in this country- the airport is now centrally located with extensive residential areas as well as industrial sites and warehouses surrounding it. Aggravating the situation is the heavy commercial traffic which takes place. It is interesting to note that last year over 200,000 takeoffs and landings were registered. This matter involves the question of public safety and is of grave concern to the people back home, and I submit it should be of grave concern to the department.
I can assure the minister that this question of public safety is not something that has arisen recently. It has existed for a long time but it came to the fore on May 26 when a four-engine York aircraft crashed in the vicinity of the airport after taking off. The aircraft took off in a northwesterly direction with the result that the crash occurred on the fringe of the airport with a tragic loss of the life of the pilot and co-pilot. If the aircraft had been taking off, as is often the case, in a southeasterly direction, such a crash might have claimed a heavy loss of life in the residential area and extensive damage to property.

On a point of order, I know that hon. members are interested in what the hon. member is saying about the recent accident at Edmonton, but at the present time it is the subject of a judicial inquiry and it seems to me that it is rather inappropriate that it should be discussed in this committee at this time.

I draw particular attention to the accident to impress upon the house the urgency of the construction of such an airport, because the matter of public safety is a primary consideration.
There are other factors, however, which necessitate early construction of this airport. The fact is that, if this airport is further delayed, it denies Edmonton the opportunity
Supply-Transport
of becoming an air transport centre of international significance. The topography, geography and the weather conditions in that area lend themselves very favourably to that.
I believe the minister is aware that many companies were interested in being located at Edmonton but, after examination of the facilities available there, were forced to take second choice. I have an interesting article here which gives evidence of this. It appeared in the Edmonton Journal of February 2, 1955.
Service by British Overseas Airways Corporation between London and Tokyo via Edmonton, and possibly London-Edmonton-Honolulu-Auckland as well.
A decided interest in the first was indicated by Sir Miles Thomas, chairman of the BOAC board, when he visited Edmonton twice in the fall of 1953. He found the municipal airport too small, too near the centre of town and too hemmed in by built-up areas, but he recognized the city's strategic position and predicted: "Within two and a half years the flying time between Edmonton and London will have shrunk to 13 hours non-stop-providing this city has long enough runways."
There is also the evidence that the Scandinavian Airlines System had made plans to be located in Edmonton. After examination of our airport facilities there, they found that these did not measure up to the requirements for long range operations and maximum load takeoffs. That particular organization switched to Winnipeg. My point is that Edmonton suffered a serious commercial loss. The argument might be made that our loss was somebody else's gain in Canada, but that is not the point at all. The fact is that the building of the new municipal airport in Edmonton would enable Edmonton, on behalf of Canada, to compete with such places as Anchorage and other cities in the United States that are bidding for consideration.
With intercontinental transport being the topic of the day, with a great deal of talk about the trans-Arctic routes, it is a question of sound economics to exploit the logical and strategical position offered in Edmonton alone. Last year the minister in a joint statement implied that such an airport would be undertaken at the earliest possible date. I quote from a news release of the British United Press of December 23, 1954:
A new major airport is to be built for Edmonton. Federal Transport Minister Marler and Mines Minister Prudham announce that orders have been given for examination of possible sites.
District officials of the transport department have been instructed to submit recommendations during the coming year with a view to an early start on the project.
On March 8, some three months after this announcement, I asked the minister what progress had been made in that regard. At that time the minister stated, as is recorded on page 1811 of Hansard of March 8, that he

Supply-Transport
was not in a position to state exactly when the commencement of the airport would take place. He said:
. . . instructions have been issued to the district officials of the Department of Transport to proceed with a detailed examination of possible airport sites in the vicinity of Edmonton and to submit recommendations in the course of 1955 as to the most suitable site with a view to an early start in construction.
Some six months following the official statement issued last year, which was made on December 21, 1954, I asked a series of questions which appeared in the Votes and Proceedings No. 103, of Thursday, June 9, 1955, page i. The first question reads as follows:
How many sites were surveyed for the construction of a new airport at Edmonton, Alberta, and what are the locations of these sites?
The second question reads as follows:
Were these contracts for surveys let by tender?
The fifth question reads as follows:
What firms submitted tenders and what was the amount of each tender?
The sixth question reads:
What firm or firms were awarded the contracts?
The seventh question reads as follows:
When is it expected these surveys will be completed and construction of the airport commenced?
The most interesting answer was the answer to No. 2, which reads:
No tenders have been called for and no survey contracts have been awarded.
The answer then said:
3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Answered by No. 2.
I should like to know at this time what amount of the estimates presently before the house is being earmarked for the construction or the survey work at that particular area. I should like to tell the minister that the people back home want that airport very badly and they are not prepared to wait indefinitely or have this matter postponed and held out as election bait before the next election. They want that airport now, and they want it for reasons of public safety and because it implies an economic potential for our community. Another thing which will interest all members in the house is that it will guarantee for Canada a proper share of the benefits accruing from intercontinental and trans-Arctic traffic. Unless we have a definite answer as to the commencing date, the tone of the editorial which appeared in the Edmonton Journal on February 2, 1955, seems to be substantiated. It reads as follows:
The city began more than five years ago to ask the. federal government for airport relocation. The civic administration, on the whole, has been determined and persistent about it. What has been obtained in all this time? Just this: a promise to

build a new airport in the future. This is an accurate measure of the federal government's capacity for talking around the point, stalling, backing and filling, and doing next to nothing of a concrete nature.
The city has endeavoured to enlist the support of the Edmonton cabinet minister, the Hon. George Prudham. The result? As above, so far.
I urge the minister to look into this matter and give it the attention that this subject deserves.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers the numerous questions and statements that have been made, I have one or two questions I should like to ask him. No doubt he is quite aware of the problem. I understand that the maintenance of way men on the Canadian National Railways made representations or had talks with the president of the Canadian National Railways regarding the fact that quite a goodly number have been laid off and contracts have been awarded for that same type of work to the R. F. Welch company. I wanted to ask the minister whether any contracts had been let for maintenance of way work to the R. F. Welch company in the area between Toronto and Windsor and from London north into the Bruce-Owen Sound area.
No doubt one of the answers will be that R. F. Welch company are prepared to do that work at less cost per mile. I would assume that would be one of the answers, although I do not know. No doubt he will have an explanation. I think the Canadian people will appreciate whatever he has to say along that line. The maintenance of way men who are capable and who have been doing that work feel let down about it because of the fact that while during the difficult war years they maintained the right of way and made it possible for the railroads to operate, now when the labour market has more men offering themselves for positions they find themselves without a job and see the work left to firms to do. I suppose that is part of the price that must be paid. However, it would seem to me that through cooperation and organization these same maintenance of way men who have been laid off could do the work. I think it is a matter of organization more than any other one thing.
While the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, would not commit himself definitely and say that no further contracts would be awarded to that company, he left the impression with them that after May 31 they would try to arrange matters so that the railway employees would be doing that work. But now I am informed that more contracts for that work have been let to the R. F. Welch company.

Just while I am on my feet I might point out that the hon. member for Oxford and one or two other hon. members also mentioned the fact that they were aware of this situation and were interested in the problem.
I think that is all I have to say. When the minister is replying to the other questions, 1 hope he will also answer that one.

I shall not detain the committee for very long. I just want to say that I have had the opportunity of getting out to the west coast and of going over the new Terrace-Kitimat construction on the Canadian National Railways. I should just like to say that it focuses attention on the development on the northern interior part of British Columbia. Following what the hon. member for Peace River said yesterday, may I say that the people in the northern interior of British Columbia are looking forward to the expenditure of public funds to the general advantage of Canada in the development of that part of British Columbia.
When one considers the matter from the standpoint of rail traffic alone and realizes that enough lumber is shipped out of Prince George during one year to build all the homes in a oity like Edmonton, one begins to realize the importance of the development of that area. When the minister makes his trip out to the west coast I am sure he will get a taste of western hospitality. If he only knew what was awaiting him, I am confident that he would not hesitate to make every possible effort to get out there at an early date.
There has been a new appointment on the Canadian National Railways to the position of superintendent in that area, with emphasis, I am sure, placed upon the improvement of the roadbed between Redpass and Prince Rupert. This indicates, of course, the fact that much more traffic is expected over that particular part of the Canadian National Railways.
I should just like to point out to the minister that the accident which occurred at the Prince George airport puts emphasis on the fact that much more money needs to be spent there. I know there is some allocation for that airport this year. I do not know just exactly what the money is to be spent for, but the fact that this accident occurred puts emphasis on the necessity for something being done to strengthen the runways of that airport. The central location of the airport in the province of British Columbia and also the weather conditions that prevail there make it one of the most important airports in western Canada.
I should also like to suggest to the minister that much encouragement should be given to small aircraft companies operating in the
Supply-Transport
northern part of British Columbia. Local air traffic should be encouraged. I think that every effort should be made to get more small companies into the flying business in connection with these short hops in British Columbia. Assistance should be given to them, and every effort should be made to help them get into the flying business and the transport business. They would work as feeder lines for the Canadian Pacific Air Lines, a company that serves the country well. I must admit that the Canadian Pacific Air Lines is doing a good job in serving that part of the country.
That brings me to the point that much improvement is needed in the airport at Quesnel. When the minister visits that western country, if he will visit the town of Quesnel I think he will find that the growth of that particular little city has been phenomenal and that improvement in the airport is certainly well warranted.
That is all I have to say with respect to conditions as far as transportation is concerned in my particular area at this time. After the dominion-provincial conferences are finished and over with, and after the minister has had a chance to get out on the ground and look the country over at first hand, I am certain that we shall be well looked after. The benefit that will come to the over-all Canadian economy from federal participation in the development in that part of the country will, I am sure, be far beyond expectations at this moment.

There is just one question I should like to ask the minister. Is there any compulsion in connection with keeping brush and scrub cut on the right of way on the railway at farm crossings? On farm land, where the railroad goes right through the farm and people have to cross the railroad, is there any compulsion about keeping the brush and weeds cut on that right of way because of the necessity of having good vision while going across the track?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to try to reply as briefly as possible to the observations which have been made by those who have participated in the general discussion on this first item of the departmental estimates. I note that some 22 hon. members have taken part in the discussion. A rather large number of points have been raised. I shall do my best to reply to the most important of them. If I do not reply to all of the observations made by all of the hon. members, I perhaps should say to them that I shall be pleased to give consideration to what they have said and, where such action would be appropriate, to draw it to the attention of the proper authorities.

Supply-Transport
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in his remarks yesterday, among other things, spoke about the increase which had taken place in some of the objects of expenditure of the department. I think that perhaps the most important criticism was that which he directed to object No. 8 which covers our expenditures for telegrams, telephones and other communication services. I think I am describing the situation correctly when I say that he expressed certain surprise that this item was to increase in the current year. When I look at the details, however, I think it is perhaps surprising there has not been a greater increase, and I think that we have been rather successful in holding down our expenditures for these purposes.
The total expenditure for this object is $3,108,000, that is to say, for communication of all kinds. I think the hon. member will realize that one cannot operate a "met" service without having communications which provide a rapid means of transmitting information from one point to another. One cannot operate a "met" service in any other way. Of the total, $1,295,000 is attributable to "met" services and of the increase an amount of less than $9,000 is applicable to this item. Other important items are aviation radio aids, $334,000, marine navigation aids, $439,000, air traffic control, $761,000, and the increase for these items is approximately $107,000. That increase is directly attributable to increased services, particularly to aviation and more particularly so far as northern development is concerned. I do not apologize for the increases. I think they are necessary. I think they are necessary to keep up with what I referred to yesterday, the growth of civil and military flying and particularly of civil flying.
If one looks at the other objects of expenditure to which the hon. member referred, civilian allowances, freight, express and cartage, office stationery, and so on, I think it will be found that the increases are attributable to an expansion of services in meteorology and in aviation and marine radio aids and for air traffic control.
The next point I want to touch on was dealt with by two hon. members, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Vancouver East. I refer to the story which appeared in the Vancouver Sun over the signature of Stanley Burke. I should like to say at the outset that when this article was drawn to our attention shortly after publication my departmental officials made a very thorough investigation into all of the criticisms which Mr. Burke had made in his article. I want to say that the investigation was made not only in our own department (Mr. Marler.]
but among those who had actually been on the voyage on which Mr. Burke had been a passenger.
I think perhaps I should point out two things to the committee in connection with what Mr. Burke has said and I shall merely read a part of a paragraph from a memorandum on the subject which says:
Mr. Burke joined the ship not when the ship sailed and when everything would be spick and span and have the best presentable public appearance, but in the middle of the northern operation. He was very antagonistic while on board ship. He tried to foist what he thought was his superior knowledge upon the master of the ship and his manner of behaviour while on board ship was not at all satisfactory to the ship's authorities.
I express no personal opinion with regard to the matter but I think that perhaps it would be desirable to realize that Mr. Burke did not come on board at the time when the ship would be in the pink of condition, and that he arrived on the ship at a time when one would not normally expect it to be in the condition in which it would have left port. I should like to deal with some of the criticisms which Mr. Burke made in his article and which were repeated in the house yesterday. The first was:
Every year she heads north with a brand new crew of political appointees . . . Almost all obtain their jobs through political influence. Few have previous sea experience.
Those are Mr. Burke's words. This statement is not in accordance with the facts. The crew of the C.G.S. C. D. Howe has been together for a number of years, and at the beginning of each season new appointments are made only for the purpose of filling vacancies. In every case the officers have the officially prescribed certificates and qualifications to perform the work for which they are employed;. In a number of cases the officers hold certificates for higher and more responsible positions than those actually held. None of them secured his appointment through political influence. A considerable proportion of the other crew members have been with the ship for a number of years. The responsibility for hiring crew members rests with the marine agent at the home port of the ship, in this case Quebec. It is the responsibility of the marine agent and master of each vessel to ensure that all crew members have the necessary qualifications and the master has absolute discretion to reject any applicant who, in his opinion, is not qualified.
Unlike commercial ships, where the crew is responsible only for the operation of the ship, the crew of the C. D. Howe when engaged in northern supply is also responsible for handling the cargo and putting it ashore at the many points at which the ship calls in the course of the voyage. Another problem in

connection with the recruitment of crews for ships such as the C. D. Howe is the fact that the work is to some extent seasonal in character. There is a regular operating crew that stays with the ship the year round but at the beginning of the season this must be supplemented to take care of the cargo handling for northern supply and the first to be hired are those who have previously served. Vacancies are filled from those best qualified for the work.
It is a fact that recommendations for employment are made from time to time by members of parliament but in every case the marine agent and master apply the test of competency and each has complete liberty to reject any applicant who, in his opinion, has not the necessary qualifications. If I may interject a personal note, I hope that hon. members of the committee will not suggest that a recommendation from a member of parliament should be regarded as a handicap. If that is to be the view of the committee, all I can say is that it would be rather surprising and I think my correspondence might diminish somewhat in volume.
But, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I have personally said to the marine agent that I wished his judgment to be exercised in the best possible way by himself and that he was to attach first importance to capability and not necessarily to the recommendations which accompanied an applicant.
That was to the marine agent in Quebec?

Yes, who is concerned with the hiring of such additional personnel each year as are required to supplement the regular crew. There is a complaint made by Mr. Burke that the officers do not hold deep-sea certificates. The answer is that a deep-sea certificate is just what the name implies, and such a certificate is necessary for officers who operate across the oceans of the world. However, such a certificate does not imply any qualification to operate in the ofttimes shallow, narrow, poorly charted and frequently dangerous waters of the north. Actual experience in these waters is the only qualification that counts, and our officers have secured their qualifications in this manner.
Mr. Burke charged also that although every man is issued a uniform, they are almost never worn. He claimed that they did not maintain the dignity of a Canadian government ship. These uniforms are issued throughout the Canadian government marine service, and on first joining a man is not given a uniform until he has served six months. The extent to which a uniform could and should be worn depends very much on 50433-412
Supply-Transport
the area in which the ship concerned is serving, and also on the kind of work the ship is doing. In the case of northern ships it would be extremely uneconomical to use these uniforms for working. As the crew spends practically their whole time working both ashore and afloat, it is understandable that they would not use them very much on a tour of duty of northern waters.
A non-commissioned officer of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, in commenting on the crew's rather nondescript outfits, said: Another excuse in their favour for wearing such clothes is the nature of the duties they were employed on, because while we were at sea they were constantly scrubbing the decks, painting the steel work and on arrival in port were employed in the discharge of all kinds of freight from coal to flour which would dirty and damage uniforms, if worn even with the use of overalls.
Then, Mr. Burke went on to use words to the effect that they were dirty, inefficient and no credit to the blue ensign of the Canadian government. Available evidence indicates that this statement is not true. The previously mentioned Royal Canadian Mounted Police non-commissioned officer, who had travelled in the north for 20 years, reported: From my experience, I would say the C. D. Howe compares most favourably with other ships operating in the north, both from the point of view of cleanliness and the way the ship was handled. A member of the crew reported that the corridor floor on the passenger deck was scrubbed three times per day, while the walls of the passenger deck were scrubbed at least once per week and the other decks received similar attention. When the ship stopped the deckhands worked around the clock unloading the freight. When at sea it would be unsafe to lower a man over the side to paint.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, it was charged that the victualling was done by the chief steward under private contract; that he is not required to bid competitively for the contract or disclose the profits and expenses; that he runs the canteen for his own profit. The facts are that the victualling contract is based on very carefully prepared estimates and that the ship's captain has the necessary authority to insist on the maintenance of the prescribed quantity and quality of food. Not one single complaint regarding the quantity or quality of the food came to the attention of the captain of the C. D. Howe during the past summer. I might add that I understand that this arrangement is standard practice. I think it is quite obvious to hon. members that it is not feasible to call for tenders

Supply-Transport
for a steward to serve on a ship such as the C. D. Howe during a northern supply mission. I will add that for the current year we have insisted that there shall be an approved standard price list for the foods served by the steward.
Finally, I should like to say a word about the "mug-ups" for the Eskimos. This is a matter of arrangement between the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the steward and is not a matter coming under the Department of Transport.
In that remark the minister is referring to the lunches?

Yes, I am referring to the lunches provided for the Eskimos.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to appear to be sidestepping the criticism that was voiced by the hon. member for Vancouver East with regard to the supply of alcoholic beverages to the C. D. Howe last summer. A return has been made showing the quantities which were supplied as ship's stores for the northern voyage last year, and I think they were given in detail last night by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Obviously, the hon. member was not familiar with the fact that the crew of the vessel varied from 68 to 76, and when the ship left Quebec she was carrying 32 passengers. En route, there were as many as 104 additional passengers picked up, and at Resolute in the far north there were actually 91 passengers and 52 stevedores. Then, too, the voyage lasted some three months.
Now, I have not been in the far north, but I would think that perhaps the passengers would not have as much to do on a cruise in the far north as they might have in the far south, and I can understand that would perhaps provide greater opportunities for cocktail hours than would be the case if they were engaged in occupations on dry land. But at all events, the number of cases of liquor that were put aboard the vessel last year does seem rather large. I may say that' in the current season, no doubt to the regret of those who are making the northern trip, the ship's captain has been instructed not to allow cases of alcoholic beverages to be shipped aboard for the benefit of those accompanying the ship. I hope that disposes of the comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, but I must say it does seem to promise a rather dry summer.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra again this year spoke of the subject of the Canadian merchant marine. He expressed understandable regret that the number of dry

cargo vessels of Canadian registry had diminished from 145, I think he said in 1948, to 18 in 1955. I do not believe the hon. member took any special pains to point out that this reduction might be explained in part by transfers from Canadian registry to United Kingdom registry, but I am not going to quarrel with him-
I gave those figures.

I am not going to quarrel with him about the reduction from 145 to 18. I should like merely to point out that, of course, when Canadian vessels are transferred to the United Kingdom registry under the transfer plan Canada does have the right to recall these ships in time of necessity. They ought not to be looked upon as if they were lost forever.
Then, the hon. member went on to criticize the failure of the government to maintain a merchant marine, but I noticed that the hon. member made no suggestions as to how this situation might be attained. I noticed that he seemed quite satisfied merely to state the facts and to make no constructive suggestions as to what might be done to achieve the objective which he had in mind. I do not say that in criticism. I have been in opposition myself, and I realize there are certain difficulties under which members of the opposition labour.
We sympathize with your difficulties, too.
Perhaps it may be difficult for the hon. member to come up with a solution that does not involve some commitment on his part to some policy.
It is up to you to announce the policy.

I used to say the same thing as that when I was in opposition; and for that reason I am not taxing the hon. member too severely, I think, for the fact that he did not at the same time produce what might be regarded as a first class solution.

That is what is called
making the best of both worlds.

And the hon. member certainly is an expert in that.
But I would like to point out that the reason for this diminution in the number of ships on Canadian registry is very simple, and that is that the standard of living in Canada is much higher than it is in the nations with which Canada would have to compete in the shipping world.
I suppose there is no market that is more international, and no field of competition that

is more international than maritime shipping; and operators of Canadian ships since the war have had to face growing competition from ships on United Kingdom registry, and on Scandinavian registry, as well as German, French, Italian, Greek and, to a growing extent, competition from ships of Panamanian and Liberian registry.
The result is that Canadian operators with vessels on Canadian registry have been under the necessity of manning their ships with Canadian officers and men, and it seems to me a most perfectly natural, human and understandable thing that Canadians who serve on Canadian vessels are anxious to make just as much money as those who are working on Canadian soil. I think that is quite understandable; and I do not believe anyone would expect a Canadian to go to sea and try to subsist on the salaries and wages that are paid to their counterparts in ships of other registries.
That is a very real handicap, but it is not of course the only one. The second report of the Canadian maritime commission made in 1949 gives some rather interesting figures with regard to the daily operating costs of a 10,000-ton dry cargo vessel. These were taken as averages for the year 1948, and perhaps can be looked upon now as being somewhat out of date. But I would refer hon. members to the second report of the commission at page 41, which sets forth some very interesting figures as to total operating costs and also, on the following page, the basic monthly wage scales paid to officers and men in such vessels.
But I would like to emphasize that from the point of view of the operator he must face not only higher operating charges, if he is going to employ a Canadian crew, but he must also expect to face higher costs for subsistence, stores, supplies, repairs, maintenance, insurance, sundries and management.

But that would not be true
in a comparison between Canadian and American costs, would it?

No; and if my hon. friend
will permit me I shall try to deal with the question of the American situation in just a moment. But the fact remains that for the causes I have just mentioned it costs probably $75,000 to $100,000 a year more under present conditions to operate a 10,000-ton dry cargo vessel on Canadian registry than it does under the other registries to which I referred a moment ago.
Some may say that $75,000 is nearer the exact figure. I shall add only that some operators have said to me that it runs to $100,000. But I do not select any particular 50433-412i
Sup p ly-Transport
figure; I merely indicate the range of opinions that have been expressed to me.
Then, referring to the competition mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, as applied to United States ships, that is one situation where the competition is on an entirely different basis. As the hon. member knows, the United States government provides subsidies toward operating costs of ships on United States registry and subsidies toward capital costs of ships built in the United States. Although the wages and salaries paid to their officers and men are higher than in Canada, the cost to the United States treasury represents a very substantial sum of money.
I do not believe however that the competition our Canadian operators have to meet is principally with United States ships because, as many hon. members know, the United States, by its program of aid to European nations and nations elsewhere, requires that half of the aid be carried in United States bottoms. When one is giving away a lot of money I suppose one can insist upon such conditions. But I think it must be remembered, when one considers the problem of Canadian shipping, that one thing that enables European countries to buy Canadian goods is the fact that they are earning money through their shipping. I am not suggesting that that is the beginning and end of the problem, but I do say it is an aspect that must not be overlooked.
Yesterday, and in the same connection, the hon. member also referred to shipbuilding. Of course I have no doubt Canadians would like Canada to have a shipbuilding industry which would build large numbers of ships and to operate a large Canadian merchant marine. But I think that while we would like to see this, we have to be realistic and remember the kind of competition we have to meet. I should say in passing that one should recall that the costs of shipbuilding in Canada are approximately 165 per cent of what they are in the United Kingdom for the same type of ship.
What about the United States?

I suppose costs are probably higher in the United States than in Canada but, as I said a moment ago, there is a capital subsidy from the United States government for people who are building ships in United States yards. And I would add one further statement on the subject. I had not been Minister of Transport very long before persons interested in Canada's shipping operations called to see me, and I may say I have received quite a number of visits from them. I can say quite truthfully that during the time I have been minister there has been no

Supply-Transport
problem which has seemed more complex and more difficult to solve than that of providing Canada with a merchant marine. Perhaps I should go on to say that these representations have continued over a long period of time, and the matter is at present under active consideration by the cabinet. At the moment I am not at liberty to disclose what recommendations I have made to my colleagues; but I am sure hon. members will understand that with three sittings of the house every day it is difficult to find sufficient time, in the intervals between sittings, to give to a problem of these dimensions the time that it merits.
Yesterday I listened with much interest to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in what he had to say about the position of the farmers owning islands in the St. Lawrence, and particularly those in the neighbourhood of Sorel. I know, just as he does, that it has been traditional for those farmers to cultivate hay and other crops on the islands of the St. Lawrence, and that it was always customary for them to transport these crops to the mainland over the ice, when it was possible to do so. I realize that the fact that it has been necessary for our icebreakers to carry their activities farther afield than in the past has caused some very real inconvenience to those farmers, and has disrupted what has been almost a traditional way of carrying on farming in that part of the province.
The great difficulty of course is to find the proper balance between the inconvenience experienced, on the one hand, by the farmers and the necessities of navigation, on the other. I should like to assure him that I listened to his representations yesterday with much interest. I shall reread them and see whether we can do something which will diminish the effects so far as these farmers are concerned.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni referred to transportation along the coastal areas of British Columbia. I think I can merely suggest to him that it would probably be desirable if those for whom he spoke were to make representations to the royal commission on coastal shipping which will sit in due course in British Columbia. I may say that the order in council appointing the commission indicates quite clearly that the commission is to be free to recommend different policies for different parts of Canada if that seems expedient.
I listened with much interest to the remarks concerning rail services to the Peace river district and transportation from Dawson Creek to the west coast. In reply to the observations of the hon. member for Peace River I can only say that the subject was the subject of a statement made by the Prime Minister on Friday, June 3, at which time

he made it known that the government proposed to pay a subsidy of $25,000 per mile for not more than 50 miles of an extension by the Pacific Great Eastern Railway northward from Prince George. The remarks of the Prime Minister will be found on page 4390 of the current edition of Hansard.
I should like to supplement what was then said by informing members of the committee that since that statement was made oral representations have been made on behalf of the government of British Columbia and it is our understanding that they are to be followed by written representations. The information which we had had before us I think is summarized in the Prime Minister's statement. It was suggested that there were other factors to which consideration should be given. As soon as we have further information and further representations from the British Columbia government the matter will be re-examined and reconsidered.
Press dispatches on the west coast indicate that the premier of British Columbia had actually written to the Prime Minister on this subject over a month ago. Are those reports inaccurate?

No, I do not think they are. I think he wrote to say that his officials were coming to Ottawa and it was following that letter that an official did come here, and he carried on discussions with the deputy minister of this department and others. It was following those discussions that written representations were expected to be made.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words of thanks for the kind remarks made by the hon. members for Roberval (Mr. Ville-neuve) and Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) with regard to the Canadian National Railways branch line between St. Felicien and Chibougamau.
I should tell them that the electors of their constituencies seem quite gratified at their efforts. In fact I have been literally flooded with letters of thanks and congratulations from municipal councils and others, from every corner of the province. I can well understand how it must pain our hon. friends opposite, but in spite of what members of the opposition might say, the bare fact remains that the people from the Lake St. John district and the surrounding area understand that the government and not the opposition must get the credit for the building of that part of the railroad.
(Text):
I was much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I realized, of course, when he expressed a some-

what subtle compliment with reference to my remarks on the subject that worse was to follow. I was not mistaken. I should like to deal perhaps as briefly as I can with some of the questions he raised.
The hon. member inquired as to the cost of the facilities in connection with this service to Port aux Basques. I should like to give him the figures as simply as possible. I shall not give the expenditure to date but rather what is considered to be the estimated total cost of the facilities at both ends so far as we can now tell. As I said in my remarks yesterday, the ferry is expected to cost about $11,500,000, the terminal facilities at Port aux Basques, $6,334,000 and the dredging, as was said before, $280,000. The facilities at North Sydney are estimated to cost $3,646,000, making an estimated total cost of $21,760,000.
The hon. member referred to the cost of breakwaters in Port aux Basques harbour. I do not think that he had heard the remarks that I had made previously with regard to what we proposed to do concerning Port aux Basques. I said yesterday that I was endeavouring to obtain the services of a competent independent expert to give us his advice as to what further works if any were necessary at Port aux Basques in order, not only that the William Carson should operate safely but that shipping should be able to operate into Port aux Basques under reasonable weather conditions.
I hope that it will be possible to have the report of this expert at an early date. I may say to hon. members of the committee that I have not yet succeeded in retaining the services of any individual although I am endeavouring to do so. Our wish is to secure somebody at once who will make an examination at once and submit an early report so that if further works are required they can be carried out promptly. Consequently in giving these figures which I have just given as to the estimated cost I should like to have it understood that if further works are required their cost was not included in the figure I just gave.
The hon. member asked for particulars of the ferry. I will not give him all of them and if there is anything I leave out I hope the hon. member will draw it to my attention. The ship will have a gross tonnage of 9,500 tons; a deadweight tonnage of 1,800 tons. It will be capable of carrying 75 automobiles, 6 trucks, 2 truck-trailers, 50 head of cattle, 650 tons of other cargo, 250 first class passengers and 50 second class passengers. She will have a complement of 90, but I think it is reasonable to say that approximately 20 of those will be required particularly because of the passenger service. I understand that in the operations to Argentia it is
Supply-Transport
intended to have a crew of about 70 and with the normal complement being 90 I infer that the crew attributable directly to the carrying of passengers might be said to be 20. I hope that that answers that question by the hon. member.
