speechtext: Before the minister proceeds to his next point, and just in order that we may not be accused of unfairness later on, may I say that it is my duty to advise the minister that he has spoken for 40 minutes. He can, of course, continue with unanimous consent.
Go ahead.
There is certainly no desire on my part to extend my remarks further. If the opposition is agreeable to my sitting down, I am quite agreeable to do so.
Stand up.
We like the sound of your voice.

The hon. member spoke about the shipping containers. My understanding is that there are at present 500, which will accommodate five tons of cargo as maximum capacity. The expected average is two tons in each container. As I understand it, there are to be 250 for Port aux Basques and 250 for North Sydney, and I am sure the hon. member will realize that there will be a great deal of interchange between the two. I understand there is approximately that number at each port. Quite obviously, if the vessel gets into operation soon at both these terminals, it may be possible that a larger number of containers will be necessary, but I understand that that is one of the necessary conditions in order to effect this rapid turnaround and effect the loading and unloading as efficiently as possible.
Has the minister the cost of those containers?

Yes, the cost of the containers is $466,000 for 500. Mr. Chairman, on the subject of the Bluenose, I would just like to say this in particular in reply to the hon. member. I hope he will be satisfied that I should not go into the details of the question. As hon. members will remember, the launching, which was originally planned for November, had to be postponed. I should say that I do not believe the fact that it was not launched made any great difference, because the shipbuilders at the time assured me it would be possible to proceed with the work during the winter as well with the ship on the slips as at the wharf.
But in view of the comments that were made at the time and in view of the delay

Supply-Transport
which took place in connection with the finishing of the ship, I should like to tell the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that I went through the pile of correspondence from beginning to end in order to find out who was responsible for the delay in the delivery of the gear boxes. I will say without any equivocation that I am quite convinced that the delay is attributable to neither the shipbuilder nor the Department of Transport. I do not want to go further than that. If the hon. member would like to see the correspondence on the matter, I would be glad to show it to him privately, but I hope I may be excused from giving any more detailed explanations. I am quite convinced that the shipbuilders were not responsible, nor was the department, for the delay in the readying of the Bluenose for service between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor.
On the question of when the ship will enter into service, I said some time ago that we feared that the difficulties that were discovered during the preliminary trials would delay the service by approximately two weeks. I am still hopeful that the estimate that was made at that time will prove to be a realistic one. I can assure hon. members that these gear boxes have been a source of a considerable number of headaches to everybody concerned, and I hope we shall find that we have some aspirin or something which will get rid of the headaches.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South touched on the question of dieselization, and I should like to say to him at once that there has never been, in my mind at least, any doubt whatever as to the capability of the shopworkers in Canadian National Railways shops or in the C.P.R. shops. I am quite satisfied that Canadian mechanics are as good as can be found anywhere. However, the problem is not one of capability. The problem is one of running the railroad as efficiently as possible, and I think we all realize that such forward steps as dieselization bring about a certain disruption. For my part I am not in a position to come to any decision about it. I should be glad to draw to the attention of the management the remarks that were made concerning the C-.N.R. shops at Winnipeg.
I should like to touch as quickly as I can on the question of the bridges in Montreal. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace referred to having what might be called uniform bridge tariffs or tolls, and he also referred to the toll collection facilities. I should like to assure him that the question of the toll collection facilities on the harbour bridge is a subject of discussion between the national harbour board and the city. I believe some 
change is to be made, and I believe it is going to be possible to make some improvements. But greater improvements are contemplated in connection with the seaway, and I do not know to what extent it is going to be possible to streamline the toll collecting facilities at the present time. But we all realize how desirable it will be to simplify them and to accelerate the movement of the traffic.
As to the question of modifying the amount of the tariff and using a simpler form of collection, I can merely point out that the question of tariffs is a subject of contract. That will have to be examined, and it is under examination, to see whether such a thing as the hon. member has spoken of is possible.
In his remarks last night the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace tried to suggest that there was a difference of opinion between myself and the Hon. Mr. Chevrier concerning the bridge facilities in Montreal. I think that arose from a complete misunderstanding by the hon. member of the articles which appeared in the Gazette yesterday morning.
I would like to say that Mr. Chevrier was expressing the opinion of the seaway authority that a third bridge at Montreal would be preferable to having a highway on top of the dike of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. That was one of the subjects which was very fully discussed with the city authorities on Tuesday morning. I think I could summarize the matter by saying that, when they left, they expressed to me their satisfaction with the discussions that had taken place.
I saw in the newspapers afterwards they had expressed that satisfaction to the reporters, and I think they had good reason to be satisfied, because we had the most friendly discussion, and I may say to the members of this committee that I promised the city that I would give immediate and sympathetic study to the new proposals which we discussed on Tuesday. But I should like the hon. member to understand that when I say "consideration", that is not the same thing as approval. He seemed to think that, because I had promised sympathetic consideration, that meant I had approved what had been suggested. If I had approved what had been suggested, I would have said so. But the fact that I did not express approval does not mean I am at the moment expressing either approval or disapproval. I have said to them that we would examine their plans sympathetically.
Perhaps I might dispense with the subject of the seaway in this general discussion. There is an item in the estimates on which hon. members may wish to make further comments. In view of the advancing hour, I

might dispense with commenting further on that subject at the moment.
The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace also spoke about a turning basin in the harbour of Montreal. I do not think that his remarks yesterday to the effect that I had not touched on the question of the effects of the seaway on Montreal were entirely justified because I went to some pains to indicate that we were effecting immediately in Montreal improvements to cost about $7 million as a first stage in a larger program in order that Montreal will maintain its position in the grain trade of Canada and so that the grain-handling facilities will be the most modern and entirely suited to the unloading of the large lakers. If I did not deal specifically with a turning basin, it was merely because a turning basin as such is not contemplated; but in the later stages of the program it is now expected that there will be a widening of the existing channel in 1956 and dredging of the approach channels to some wharves and that these operations will be carried out probably in 1956 and 1957.
Then there is the subject of C.N.R. equipment. I may say that I was sorry the hon. member felt it necessary to express words of criticism about the equipment of the C.N.R. Quite candidly I do not share his views on the subject and I doubt whether they would be shared by persons who have travelled on both transcontinental trains. Actually it is a fact that the railway company has spent something like $75 million in the last three years in order to provide new equipment and it has bought more than 500 new units. I had the opportunity personally of inspecting both Canadian National Railways equipment and Canadian Pacific Railway equipment. From the point of view of comfort, I think that neither railway can say that it has better equipment than the other. There are two differences. One is that the C.P.R. has gone in for stainless steel exteriors on its equipment. I think that is a matter of taste. I do not think that it either adds to or subtracts from the comfort of those who are travelling.
As far as the vista-dome cars are concerned, which the C.P.R. has and which the C.N.R. has not, that subject was discussed before the sessional committee. Mr. Gordon said that the question was carefully considered by the management of the railway and that it was not convinced that the extra cost would produce extra revenues or extra comfort which would be commensurate with the additional expense. I should like to add that a number of my friends who have travelled across Canada since the faster services were inaugurated have said that they found that both trains were comfortable indeed.
Supply-Transport
I hope that the hon. member will adopt a fairer attitude to the C.N.R. Perhaps if he travels around more, he will find that what I have just said is fully justified.
One of the hon. members spoke about smoke from shipping in Toronto. I should merely like to say that the international joint commission has a continuing committee on the subject and that I do not think that, at the moment at least, it calls for any legislative action.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke about the coal-fired turbine and the matter of coal supplies for the Canadian National Railways. I think some of these questions relate more directly to matters under the control of my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; but so far as the C.N.R. aspects of the matter are concerned, I shall be glad to draw them to the attention of the management.
Perhaps the question of the decision in the Associated Airways case is one with which I might deal on some other item in the estimates. I should like to reply more fully to the hon. member for York West. I believe there is a good reply to be made to him but, having regard to the time, perhaps it would be more agreeable to him that we resume the discussion on air policy on some item in connection with air services.
I certainly do not want to miss answering the question asked by my friend the hon. member for Greenwood. I should like to demonstrate that, when questions are clearly put, I do my best to understand them, at any rate, even if I am not always successful. The first question he asked was about the director of economic policy. He is Mr. George Scott who was formerly attached to the board of transport commissioners but who is now attached to the department. He advises us on matters concerning the board of transport commissioners; he is available to the board of transport commissioners in like manner and also to the air transport board; and in a general way he deals with the economic aspects of the numerous transportation problems that come before the department from time to time. Perhaps the title may be misleading. But Mr. Scott is a most capable economist and I must say that I found most helpful his reports on the economic aspects of various transportation problems.
So far as Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships are concerned, as I told the sessional committee the matter is under consideration. There is at present an interdepartmental committee which is studying the question. I know how desirable it would be if we could come to a decision as to the term

Supply-Transport
during which this service was to be continued. That matter was under discussion in the sessional committee. I am hopeful that, when the interdepartmental committee has completed its study, we shall be able to make a more definite statement on the question.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word in reply to the hon. member ' for Edmonton East and to say to him that a statement was made concerning the Edmonton airport earlier this year. I should like to submit that there has been no stalling whatever on the part of my department or its officials; that about a dozen sites in the vicinity of Edmonton have been intensively examined; and that there has been made to the department a report which is now under consideration. It is not just a matter of picking out any area of land and saying "Let us make an airfield out of it". It is not a matter of calling for tenders. The preliminary work is done by officials of the department. When the hon. member put his question, it was quite clear that he did not realize the method which the department follows in establishing an airfield. But I can assure him-just as I have already assured my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, who have shown a real interest in the matter-that we are getting on with this work, that we are ahead of schedule, and that we are ahead of the promises which we made to the municipal authorities of Edmonton last year.
Earlier, before this debate began, the hon. member for Winnipeg South talked about the Welch company contracts and the hon. member for Middlesex East spoke about them. I should merely like to say that, as Mr. Gordon has said, the existing contracts were terminated at the end of May. Some further contracts have been given by tender. I believe other contracts may have been given by arrangement. But I should like to point out that these contracts relate not to the maintenance of the right of way but rather to the operation of laying rails and ballasting.
I think I have covered perhaps briefly but I hope not too summarily the questions that have been raised. I would hope that it would now perhaps be possible to pass the first item.
Will the minister answer the question I asked him? It will take him only a minute.

Yes. I am sorry I did not cover it. Perhaps I should have said to the hon. member that I am unable to answer

the question at this moment but I will try to get the information and communicate it to him, perhaps privately.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall resolution 449 carry?
Carried.
One o'clock.

I should like to ask the minister some questions with reference to boats and trips up north to which reference has been made. I would ask you to call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

I did not want to interfere with the minister when he was making his statement this morning but I should like to refer to the first part with reference to the trips north on the boat that was referred to by one hon. member as being loaded with liquor and Liberals.
Not Liberals, liquor.
I understood he said liquor and Liberals.
I do not recall that. I can see no connection between the two either.
I understand these are summer jobs?

Not at all. I went over that very fully this morning. I tried to make it perfectly clear to the committee that for the most part the members of the crew are permanent, that some are added each year but that as to those engaged each year those who have been there before are given the preference. In other words, experience is the principal qualification for those who are hired.

I am glad the minister has explained that because a defeated Liberal candidate in my riding was on one of these trips to the north this summer, and I would hate to think he was appointed for patronage reasons because he is a good dentist.

I am sorry the hon. member was not listening to me this morning but I can assure him that, so far as I am concerned, in the choice of those having summer jobs there is no question of patronage whatever. When it comes to people of professional qualifications I think our difficulty has been to get them rather than to find out whether they were Liberals, Conservatives, Social Crediters

or something else. I can tell my hon. friend quite plainly that that is not one of the necessary qualifications. Of course I am inclined to think that more intelligent people are found with Liberal leanings.
I can tell the minister I think he has very bad judgment in that respect, particularly so if he goes around my riding. Would these jobs be open to university students?

I do not think the kind of jobs we are talking about are those for university students. However, there are a few positions each year in that category which have been filled, and if next year the hon. member has political supporters he would like to have make a summer trip up north I would be most interested in having his recommendations.

I do not know whether or not they are political supporters. They are probably not old enough to vote yet, but I happen to have a boy going to university who tried all over Canada to get a job with one of the government services this summer.
I hope if the hon. member's son is interested next summer the hon. member will advise me of that fact in due time.

Would the minister enlarge a little on his reply regarding maintenance of way work? I inquired if any contracts had been let to the Welch company in western Ontario between Toronto and Windsor and between London, Owen Sound and Kincardine.

I remember the hon. member's question. I tried to explain that as I understand the matter the contracts apply to ballasting and rail laying. I do not think they are intended to apply to the ordinary maintenance of way operations. I am sorry that I am not able, without making inquiries from the railroad, to say whether any of these contracts affect parts of the lines which the non. member mentioned. If the hon. member is interested, I shall try to make some inquiries and let him have the information privately, but I am afraid I cannot furnish it now.

Can the minister say what stage the negotiations with the union have reached regarding the use of this company and the type of work they are doing which in the opinion of the union should be done by the regular employees?

All I can say in reply to that question is that the subject was, of course, discussed in the sessional committee, and I think there was some mention of the discussions that have taken place between the management and the unions concerning the
Supply-Transport
Welch contracts. But Mr. Gordon informed me in conversation quite recently, within the last two weeks, that there had been no particular representations made in recent weeks with regard to the contracts which, as I mentioned this morning, were awarded in some instances after tenders had been invited. I might say that the Welch company is not the only one. I believe the Rayner company is another one. There have been several of these contracts awarded, and as I understand the situation no direct representations against them have been made by the union in recent weeks.

There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister arising out of the answers he gave to my remarks yesterday. First of all, with regard to the government vessel, the C. D. Howe, what changes were made in the method of operating that ship this summer compared with the method last summer?
I take it my hon. friend's question is related to the victualling arrangements?
All the points that were discussed yesterday and today.

I think that is the only change that has resulted from this reconsideration. As I said this morning, there is a standard set of prices which has now been made subject to approval. The other change I referred to was the question of shipping cases of liquor aboard. That is really a deprivation for the passengers more than those who operate the ship.
Has the minister's department given any instructions concerning boat drills, for example, on the C. D. Howe?

Those are standing instructions. I hope, Mr. Chairman, we are not going to have to go into the whole subject of that article all over again. It covered a lot of matters which the hon. member did not raise yesterday and which I did not attempt to cover this morning. I really could have said a great deal more. I know the subject of boat drills was mentioned in the article and the hon. member did not mention it, but, as I say, there are standing instructions with regard to boat drills. I think I should also say that the criticisms of boat drills made in the article are not more founded than the other criticisms to which I referred.
The minister is deprecating this article-

Very much.

Supply-Transport
Very much, he says. Yet he admits himself that this year he has made a change with regard to liquor.
That was not even mentioned in the article.
It was mentioned in the article this spring.
But not in the article we are talking about.
Last year large quantities of liquor were put on board the ship. I understand there has also been a change with regard to the victualling. The minister just admitted that a moment ago.
In the canteen prices.
That, of course, was one of the subjects dealt with in Mr. Burke's article. Is it a fact that there was an investigation conducted by the minister's department?
I said that this morning.
Would you let us have a copy of the report?
No.
Would the minister file a copy of the report?
No, I will not.
The minister has a report on this investigation?

Well, Mr. Chairman, I have had several reports from the officials of my department on this question, just as I have had on a number of other questions. I do not think there is any suggestion that I should deposit them on the table of the house.
The minister would not be willing to file any of those reports?
I do not see any reason why I should. I could file all sorts of reports, but I do not think matters concerning internal administration of the department should be disposed of in that way.

I would have thought the minister would have taken this article a great deal more seriously than he appears to have done. His reply today, in the main, consisted I understand of reading a report he had obtained, presumably from one of his officials whJch condemned Mr. Burke. It said that this journalist was antagonistic on this trip and that he tried to force his views on them.
Foist, I said.

Then the minister went on to say that Mr. Burke had not arrived on this ship until she had been at sea for some time.

Incidentally, he used that as an excuse for the dirty appearance of the ship. He did not question that the appearance of the ship was dirty, and that it had not been kept up. He said when she left the port of Quebec she was in good shape and Mr. Burke should have reported her condition then instead of when he got on the ship some time later. I think the minister should explain to the committee a little further just why this ship, which I believe he said today is a ship of
9,000	tons-
I did not say any such thing.
What were the figures?
I did not give the figures.
He gave the gross tons and the net tons-
I was speaking about the William Carson.
Well, what is the size of this ship?
I am sorry, but I have not the figure immediately available.
In any event, it is quite a large ship. The minister did not deny that the crew members were hired on a patronage basis.
I thought I had, very formally.
He said, what was wrong with getting a letter from a Liberal member.
I did not say any such thing. I said I did not look upon a letter from a member of parliament as a handicap.
Then, a few moments ago he told the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) that if he put in a letter it might be possible to get a man hired.
We were talking about summer employment for students when I made that reply to the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.).

The only qualification for employment on a ship going into these dangerous waters should be some sort of experience at sea. The minister said that the district marine agent at Quebec city hires these people. I have turned up the annual report, and I find at page 86:
The district marine agents represent the department in matters pertaining to the marine services branch within the districts defined above, which encompass the coastline and all the navigable inland waters of Canada. They direct and administer activities pertaining to the construction, operation and maintenance of aids to navigation, the operation of marine services ships, the administration and maintenance of government wharves, public harbours and life-saving stations, the supervision of ice-breaking by contract or by government ships, except in the St. Lawrence river.

The minister made no statement this morning that one requirement for employment on this vessel was deep-sea experience; that requirement was conspicuously absent from the qualifications he mentioned. I urge upon him that in the future the policy adopted by the department for engaging men to serve on ships of this type should be that they have had some deep-sea experience. This business of getting a job with a letter from an M.P. is a very poor way to man any ship, government or otherwise, and sooner or later is bound to result in disaster. I hope that is not the way in which merchant seamen are hired for government ships on the west coast.
One other thing I think the minister should explain further is his remark that it was not essential for the officers of this ship to have deep-sea certificates. He said that deep-sea certificates were all right for crossing the Atlantic.
I did not put it in those terms, certainly.

Here these men are operating ships into far more dangerous waters than the waters of the Atlantic and the minister, whose department is responsible for seeing that no ships leave port without properly licensed officers, says that so long as these men have had experience in the north they do not need to have deep-sea certificates. We have several thousand Canadians with experience in the merchant navy during war years and the years immediately following, men who are duly qualified, and I think the minister should explain why his department does not insist that the officers of the C. D. Howe hold proper deep-sea certificates in just the same way as ships plying out of the ports of Vancouver or Halifax in regular commercial trade have to have officers with deep-sea certificates. There really is no excuse for allowing a practice of that kind to be followed. If Mr. Burke's article were of no value for any other reason, it is of great value in drawing the attention of the minister and his department, and the public of Canada, to the fact that the ship sailed last year without officers who have deep-sea certificates.
There is one other thing. This article indicates that the victualling was turned over to a contractor; that the steward was allowed to victual the ship. This year his wings have been clipped a bit by setting the price he can charge in the ship's canteen. Why does the government not purchase the goods and engage a steward in the same way they would engage other officers on the ship? It seems to me that would at least get away from the possibility of the steward making
Supply-Transport
profits which should not be paid. The article stated that last year the steward was allowed to charge 40 cents for giving an Eskimo a mug of tea and a couple of ship's biscuits. Apparently this year there has been a change and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is putting up proper box lunches.
The steward is doing it for the department.

The steward is now doing that for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. There is another beneficial result flowing from the article which was written by Mr. Burke. I hope the minister will answer these further questions, and will see that in future this ship is operated on the same basis as any other deep-sea ship would be operated.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to prolong this discussion more than is necessary. But the reason I mentioned the fact that Mr. Burke had joined the ship after she left Quebec, and that the condition was not the same as when she left port, was that I thought that perhaps would excuse some of the things Mr. Burke had said. But there were other newspapermen aboard, and I might say that we did not receive the same sort of articles from their pens as we did from the pen of Mr. Burke.
That does not prove anything.

No more than Mr. Burke's article does, either.
I would like to go back to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, who seems to suggest that the ship's officers did not have the proper qualifications. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that bears no relation whatsoever to the facts connected with the operation of the C. D. Howe.
As I said this morning, in every case the officers have the officially prescribed certificates and qualifications to perform the work for which they are employed. In a number of cases the officers held certificates for higher and more responsible positions than those actually held. And I added that none of them secured his appointment through political influence.
And then the hon. member seems to have forgotten that I dealt this morning with the question of the deep-sea certificate. That is exactly what the name implies. It is the certificate necessary for officers who operate across the oceans of the world. As I said this morning, such certificate does not imply any qualification to operate in the oft-times shallow, narrow, poorly charted and frequently dangerous waters of the north.

Supply-Transport
Actual experience in these waters is the only qualification that counts. And our officers have secured their qualifications in this manner.
I would say that the record of performance of the C. D. Howe last summer is excellent proof of the efficiency of the crew and the officers; and the fact that the northern supply program is to be even more extensive this year is further proof that we believe that the operation was successfully and efficiently carried out last year.
So far as the members of the crew are concerned, I said this morning that a considerable proportion of the crew members have been with the ship for a number of years. The responsibility for the hiring of crew members rests with the marine agent at Quebec, and it is his responsibility and the responsibility of the master to ensure that all crew members have the necessary qualifications.
I went on and said this to the committee this morning, that I had personally said to the marine agent at Quebec that capability was to be the first requirement. And I can assure the hon. member that the charge that these are political appointments is entirely without foundation.

Why not make it a rule that men employed on this and other government vessels doing similar work must be men who have had some experience at sea? Is there any reason why a rule of that kind could not be adopted, particularly in view of the fact that so many thousands of Canadian merchant seamen have been put on the beach as a result of the fading away of the merchant navy?

Last year's complement consisted of 69 persons who had previously participated in this kind of operation. There were 12 new hands-sailors-and there were four students. In the face of these facts I do not think the hon. member should insist upon talking about incompetent crews, political appointments and so on.
Has the department any plan jnder which it keeps in employment or seeps contact with trained seamen for these vessels, or are they all just picked up in this way every year?

As I said this morning-and I shall repeat it for the hon. member's benefit- there is a regular operating crew that stays with the ship the year round. But at the beginning of the season this crew must be supplemented to take care of the handling of cargo for northern supplies. Those first to be hired are the ones who have served

previously, and vacancies are filled with those best qualified for the work. What could be more clear than that?

The other question about which I would question the minister further has to do with Canada's deep-sea merchant navy. Yesterday I read to the minister from the annual report of the Canadian maritime commission, and referred particularly to page 24, where it indicates that the direct trade from the ocean, up through the St. Lawrence canal and the great lakes, now appears to be done exclusively by ships other than Canadian or United States flag ships. The report indicates that last year 99 ships, none of which was under Canadian or United States registry, made 275 trips from overseas ports to the great lakes. Then the report lists the nations to which those ships belong- Germany, 39; Norway, 33; Sweden, 12; Holland, 9; United Kingdom, 4; France, 2. Then it goes on to say that those outside lines will be operating during 1955, and that many of the lines are exploring this route in preparation for the new St. Lawrence seaway.
In dealing with the merchant navy the minister did not touch upon that aspect of the matter. Are we in Canada to be in the position, when this great seaway is completed, where no Canadian flag ships will be using the seaway? I am referring to that part from the deep sea and up through the great lakes. It would appear that such will be the case unless the government adopts some policy which will result in the re-establishment of a Canadian merchant navy. I believe the minister's remarks this morning could be summed up to the effect that because the Canadian standard of living is higher than that of other countries having merchant fleets, therefore it is very doubtful whether we should have a deep-sea fleet of our own.
I do not think that interpretation could be put upon what I said.

Well, that is what it amounted to, Mr. Chairman; and that is the type of policy the government is following at the present time. In other words, they are just letting this merchant navy die out. It is not as though Canadian trade was being carried by United Kingdom ships. The report of the Canadian maritime commission dealt with that subject, too. I pointed out yesterday the percentage of our trade carried in Canadian ships as being, in 1953, only about 4 per cent. At one time quite a large portion of this trade was carried in United Kingdom bottoms. But they have been losing out, too; and now-the minister will correct

Supply-Transport
me if I am wrong-the percentage carried by Mr. Green: Is it not a fact that the Ger-ships other than Canadian and other than mans are planning to build ships for the St. United Kingdom is 61-7 per cent. That was Lawrence seaway trade while Canada is in 1953.	doing nothing about it?
I think that is correct.

I have no doubt that the figure is higher now so that both Canadian and British ships have been steadily losing out in the carrying of our trade. The time element is most important. The minister has stated that the government is considering whether it will do something about this problem but I would point out to him that delay may make it impossible to re-establish the Canadian merchant navy. I hope that the government will make up its mind without holding over the matter for a period of months or years. Will the minister comment on this situation which appears to be arising in connection with trade through the St. Lawrence seaway into the great lakes?

Mr. Chairman, I think there is a very simple explanation. In the first place ships of either Canadian or United Kingdom registry built for the overseas trade are of too deep a draft to use the present canal. The foreign deep-sea vessels that are now plying the St. Lawrence into the great lakes are of relatively small displacement, much smaller than the deep-sea vessels under Canadian registry. I think that that is the explanation; the fact is that foreign nations have the small ships while Canadian deep-sea vessels are too large to use the canals.
So far as the proportion of Canadian overseas trade carried by ships of other registry is concerned, I do not think that I would challenge the percentages given by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra but I think that it is significant that Canadian flag and United Kingdom flag participation has dropped steadily since 1948 whereas ships of registry where conditions of employment are not so good, where wages and salaries are lower, have been gaining. For instance, and I do not say this in any critical way, ships of Panamanian and Liberian registry represented only 2-6 per cent in 1948 and they are now up to 10-7 per cent. I think that in that fact there is a very clear implication that the operating conditions of particular registers have a very profound influence upon the operation of merchant ships. The basic difficulty so far as the Canadian merchant marine is concerned is the high level of salaries and wages and other annual costs which must be paid by the Canadian operator and which are not paid in the same degree by ships of other registry, and I cite as an example those under the Liberian and Panamanian flags.

I said this morning that it costs 165 per cent to build a ship in Canada compared with what it costs in England, and I understand that in Germany the cost would be even less. Undoubtedly that gives an advantage over Canadian ships. As my hon. friend knows, the whole question of coastal shipping is being considered by a royal commission.
Not deep-sea shipping.

F. Welch company. As he knows, however, the union is capable of doing both of these classes of work, and in former times has done both of these classes of work. For my part that is the most serious aspect of this matter. I hope that it will be looked at

again, both in the light of what president Donald Gordon said to the committee earlier this year and in the light of what I am sure are repeated representations by the union. I understand, for example, that recently another encroachment has been made in that, when these contracts were first let out to the R. F. Welch company, the foremen and machine operators assigned to the Welch contract gangs were supplied by the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees. I understood, however, that there has been a change even there and that the Welch company is now permitted to hire its own supervisors and its own machine operators, although they are using equipment owned by the Canadian National Railways.
As the minister knows, some of us have raised this on a number of occasions with the Minister of Transport, and we have also asked the Minister of Labour if an inquiry should not be made into this whole matter. I suggest to the minister that there is enough concern about this whole situation that it calls for better treatment than we have yet received at the hands of the president of the Canadian National Railways in committee or in the replies that have been given by the minister on the floor of the house. I do not expect anything more out of him today, but I hope that, as soon as his estimates are out of the way and he can attend to this matter, he will go into it very thoroughly.
While I am on my feet, I wish to make one other plea to the Minister of Transport. He made reference earlier today to complimentary remarks that were made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, which he enjoyed but which he knew would be followed by something else. Perhaps I shall follow suit to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. We in this house are impressed with the efficiency of the Minister of Transport, with the way in which he has taken command of a tremendous job, and with his performance on the floor of the house. He wins deserved plaudits for his great facility in both of the official languages of the house. However, when it comes to this question of the amount of pension being received by retired C.N.R. employees, he has not shown any of that ability, efficiency, facility or imagination that we see in him with respect to some other matters.
He knows how these things work. He knows that, if an organization writes him a letter and he writes a reply, sooner or later both of those letters are seen by people who are interested. I have seen copies of a number of letters that the Minister of Transport has written to organizations representing retired C.N.R. employees. They are
Supply-Transport
the same stereotyped, stilted letters that were written, I presume, by someone in the department for his predecessor. As I read the letters, it strikes me he has not faced up to this problem at all. He has not tried to see the plight of these people on $25 a month. He gives the same old answers, without any encouragement, without even the suggestion that he is willing to look into the matter, that have been given on former occasions.
Let us not have any more of the argument that this is a contractual arrangement and that it is not the government's fault that conditions have changed and other pensions have gone up. Let us not have any more of the argument that once pensions have been fixed they cannot be increased. A great many instances can be found of pensions which have been increased because the cost of living has gone up, the standard of living has gone up or for other reasons the amount is no longer adequate.
As a matter of fact, there is one case, if not two, in the minister's estimates where the amount of pension has been increased because the amount originally decided on is recognized as inadequate. I have referred in the course of this session to an increase that was made in the pensions of retired school teachers in the province of Ontario. Again, this is a case of teachers who were on pension a number of years ago. The amount of their pension was determined by the situation at the time. It was a matter of a contractual arrangement. But it has been recognized by the province of Ontario that that pension is inadequate.
At least two provinces in this country have increased the pensions of retired civil servants in the lower brackets. I could quote instances in other countries as well. I know of at least a few instances of private employers and I know of instances of unions that pay pensions where, with the rising cost of living, pensions have been increased. These increases were not just for those who go on pension in this day and age. The pensions of those formerly retired have been increased to meet today's conditions. I am not going to burden the house with the figures; they are on the record because of answers the minister has given to questions I have placed on the order paper. But I submit it is not fair to refuse to do anything about the plight of thousands of retired C.N.R. workers being asked to get by on $25 a month.
May I ask the minister, once we get through with the estimates, and he has a little free time, to take an honest imaginative, understanding look at this problem and see if there is not some way that the pensions of our retired C.N.R. employees can be increased to a more reasonable figure.

With regard to the R. F. Welch Company contracts, I might say that I have certainly had about 20 letters in the last two weeks with regard to the matter. What I want to ask the minister particularly about is this. Has the Department of Transport any plans at present under way for any form of coastguard service on the great lakes or anything resembling it?

I think I should say that the answer to that question is no. I have a memorandum on the subject which starts off by saying that the subject was reviewed a number of years ago. At that time I am told that the conclusion that was reached was that it would cost approximately $9 million at that time for the capital expenditures necessary to start a coastguard service and that thereafter the annual cost would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3 million. I do not want, particularly at this stage of the estimates, to go into the matter too fully; but it has been pointed out to me that the R.C.A.F. undertakes basic search and rescue responsibility and that both the R.C.N. and the Department of Transport as well as other government departments such as the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the R.C.M.P., because of the ships they operate, are all able to assist in this work. The R.C.N. has numerous escort and patrol vessels which are able to perform the same sort of services. The Department of Transport maintains a fleet for northern supply. In fact, I think I could go on to show that while it has not the name of a coastguard service, the various agencies of government are so organized that a fairly good job is being done having regard to the tremendous length of coast line, interior and exterior, that has to be considered.

Just one further question. This memorandum to which the minister has just referred surely does not apply to the great lakes. It must apply to discussion of coastguard service generally on the Atlantic and Pacific as well, surely.

I should like to ask a number of questions about the St. Lawrence seaway and in order to facilitate business I think it might be appropriate if I were to put them

Supply-Transport
in point form. Since there is no estimate this year for St. Lawrence seaway surveys, investigations and design, I should like to ask the minister the following questions. First, has the department made any investigation into the effects of the seaway on other transportation systems in Canada? Second, has any survey been made with respect to the general economic effects on the future of Canada as a result of the construction of the seaway? Third, has the government any plans at the moment for deepening the St. Clair river to a depth of 27 feet? I understand the present channel has a depth of 23 to 25 feet. In the same connection, are any plans under way at the present time to deepen the Welland canal to the required depth of 27 feet? I understand some dredging is necessary to do that. Fourth, have any surveys been made by the department with respect to the probability that harbours on the great lakes, lake Ontario, lake Erie and so on, will have to be deepened in the future to accommodate the vessels which are likely to come from abroad through the seaway with the new draft? Fifth, have any studies been made with respect to the possible advisability of providing a 35 foot depth for the seaway rather than a 27 foot depth, as is apparently planned at the moment? Sixth-
Perhaps we might deal with the first five questions to start with and then the hon. member can come to the second five.
There are only two more.

First of all, so far as the
economic effects of the seaway are concerned I should say to my hon. friend that the seaway authority itself in the determination of tolls naturally has got to consider all the economic effects of the seaway on transportation in Canada. I do not think that I should consider other special surveys but I do say that the seaway authority has that particular responsibility and is engaged in that activity at the present tune. The second question was with regard to harbours. I think I should point out to the hon. member that the present state of affairs is that from the Welland canal west navigation is considered at the present time to be fairly deep water. As the hon. member knows, the lakers, particularly those engaged in the grain traffic, have a draft for the most part of about 25 feet or perhaps a little less, and the harbours on the great lakes that are accustomed to that traffic have the necessary depth for these purposes.
What we are now in the process of doing is deepening the waterway between Prescott and the port of Montreal, and in effect we are providing a means of access for deep-sea shipping to the great lakes. I understand that

some representations have been made by harbours of the great lakes that would like to see their facilities improved and deepened. I do not want to give the hon. member the impression that this is a final decision by any means, but I think one would wish to feel very certain that the traffic was going to be there before one undertook to make the large expenditures that would be required in order to provide deep draft facilities in many more harbours on the great lakes.
The hon. member asked about the depth of navigation. I understand that the possibility of 35 foot navigation was considered but was rejected, and it was thought we should go on with 27 foot navigation.

With regard to what the minister has just told us, is there any report that could be tabled and made available to members of the house that has been prepared by the seaway authority with respect to the economic effects on Canada generally?

There is no specific report to which I could refer the hon. member. Perhaps I might reply to one other question I should have dealt with, the matter of dredging in the St. Clair river, in fact, in the upper section of the waterway. I would merely remind the hon. member that traditionally the dredging in the St. Mary river, the Detroit river, lake St. Clair and the St. Clair river has been done in the past by the United States authorities and not by Canada.

I take it we should interpret the minister's last remark as meaning that the eventual deepening of the St. Clair river will probably be the responsibility of the United States and not of Canada. There are two other questions I should like to ask the minister. Can the minister give us any statement with respect to the policy that the department may be likely to follow as to seaway tolls? Can the minister give us a breakdown of the various products involved in the estimate of about 31 million tons annually that it is expected will be transported through the seaway?

I am not in a position to give the information which the hon. member has just asked for because, as I said earlier, the matter is currently under study by the seaway authority and I am not in a position to give him particulars because the work is actually being undertaken at the present time. However, if the hon. member will examine the provisions of the act concerning the St. Lawrence seaway authority he will find there provision with regard to tolls. Likewise, if he will examine the United States legislation concerning the St. Lawrence

seaway development corporation he will see that there are also express provisions there. The question of the application of tolls to individual items of traffic naturally must be the subject of study and, I would say also, a matter of discussion between the United States and Canada.

Then, one final question
in this regard. There are two parts to it. There is no appropriation this year for St. Lawrence investigation and surveys. Have the seaway engineers looking into this completed their work or has it been transferred to some other branch?

I said yesterday that the 175 employees who formerly were with the Department of Transport had been transferred to the St. Lawrence seaway authority. Of course, during the current year the charges that were formerly paid out of the Department of Transport estimates are being paid out of the loans to the seaway which are, of course, a part of the capital cost.

Then, my last question, Mr. Chairman. As a result of the work of these 175 employees who have been transferred to the authority, has there been no report that could be tabled and made available to members regarding the economic defects of the seaway or anything such as that?

I think, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member is under a misapprehension with regard to the order of importance of the various aspects of the seaway. Surely, it would be most undesirable if the seaway authority did other than concentrate its attention on building the seaway first. I do not mean they should build the seaway before they think about tolls or tariffs, but I mean placing as the first item of importance the actual building operations and then the subsidiary matters such as tolls. I do say to my hon. friend that the question of tolls and economic effects is under consideration, but as I said earlier there is no report that I could table.

Possibly the minister may have misunderstood what I meant. I said "surveys"-surely, when you have a number of people employed in looking into a certain matter it would be advisable to make certain surveys before construction was started. It is my understanding, I do not believe it was the Department of Transport but the Department of Trade and Commerce, several years ago made a report concerning the economic advantages expected to accrue to the various sections of Canada from the opening of the seaways-something to that effect. I believe a request was made for this report last year, but it was not tabled in the house. I was

I should like to touch briefly on two matters to which I have referred on two previous occasions. My first point is with regard to the great obstruction to vehicular traffic crossing the Welland ship canal which exists at Homer. The raising and lowering of the bridge impedes the constant flow of traffic. This condition has been greatly aggravated during the summer months by reason of the tourist traffic proceeding from across the river at Fort Erie and at Niagara Falls from the United States and the traffic proceeding from Canada into the United States. Many and long delays occur at this point. One would not have to be an engineer to realize that a permanent cure could only be effected by building an overhead bridge or a tunnel at this point. I believe a very practical suggestion has been made, and that is to permit three lanes of traffic to cross the bridge at busy times. This traffic would be electrically controlled. I think it would avoid a great deal of the congestion at the busier ends of the bridge, and would do a great deal to alleviate the trouble that exists at the present time. I have fears, and I am not alone in my fears, that a serious accident will occur at this point and loss of life might result. I am sure that something could be worked out to solve this difficulty.
My second point has to do with cleaning up the second Welland canal. I shall not attempt today to elaborate on the needs of this proposal. The passage of accumulated wastes through the towns of Thorold and Merritton, the city of St. Catharines and the township of Grantham causes great inconvenience to the citizens. The obnoxious odours coming from this water cause great hazard to health. Early this spring two young children lost their lives in this old canal. The cleaning up of this old canal would provide a scenic driveway and create a beauty spot in the centre of this area.

Supply-Transport
I might mention another point with regard to the cleaning up of this old canal. Next week the Royal Canadian Henley regatta will be held on the waters of the old Welland canal at Port Dalhousie. The clean-up of the canal would do a great deal to rehabilitate the course of the Royal Canadian Henley which attracts prominent oarsmen from various parts of Canada and the United States every year, who come together to vie for sculling honours. This is the finest course in North America, but it is quickly filling in with waste. The accumulation of waste makes rowing most difficult on this course. Last year two of the rowing clubs which took part in the competition damaged rather expensive shells. I am sure that when the clean-up takes place the dredging of this course will do much for rowing in Canada. I am pleased to know that the minister expects to visit this area within the next month or six weeks. I am sure the residents of the area will give him a great welcome at that time. Not only will we show him some of the problems which I have pointed out and which will confront him, but he will have the opportunity of seeing the natural beauty that we have in the Niagara peninsula at this time of year.

On previous occasions during this session, Mr. Chairman, the hon. members for Lincoln, Niagara Palls and I have presented to the members of this house some of the difficulties we experience in the Niagara district because of the presence of the Welland canal and its operation. Today the hon. member for Lincoln outlined two of our problem's. I might say these difficulties were rather fully covered during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and again when municipal grants were discussed in the house. Today I do not propose to do much more than enumerate those difficulties.
Traffic congestion in Welland and Port Colborne and particularly in the city of Welland is a very serious matter. By actual count the bridges are up one-quarter of the time or six hours out of the 24. This affects the economy of the city; it is a nuisance to the inhabitants, and it costs them money. The local taxpayers have to maintain duplicate firefighting services on each side of the canal, and they must maintain sewage disposal units on each side of the canal. The bottleneck of traffic at the Homer bridge, to which the hon. member for Lincoln referred today, is one of the worst in the country. This year I have seen cars lined up for a distance of four or five miles back.
The matter of the old canal clean-up affects four municipalities in the counties

of Welland and Lincoln. Unsanitary conditions exist there; odours have been created, and have been aggravated by the fact that the Department of Transport has cut down the flow in order to make available to the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario more water for the development of power.
This canal is not the natural drainage for all parts of that area. In some municipalities, particularly in my own town of Thorold, we have to pump the sewage and some of the water up a distance of 40 feet into the canal. If we had our own natural drainage system we would not have this expense. The expense amounts to about $20,000 a year. The reason our own natural drainage is not available to us is due to the location of the new or present Welland ship canal.
I might say in this connection that, even though a third of the land in our municipality is owned by the Department of Transport-something over 500 acres out of 1,500 -we do not come under the Municipal Grants Act in the matter of payments. I understand that is because all aids to shipping are exempt under that act. However, we feel that with a third of the land in that position we should get some payment. It seems that we do not come within the terms of the act regardless of local circumstances.
We are continuing, as we have done for the last hundred years, to supply the Department of Transport with free police and free fire-fighting services. I might say that we have drainage problems in other parts of the canal because there were not enough underpasses made for drainage when the canal was built. In some areas the water in the canal is higher than the surrounding area. In other places, where drainage can take place into the canal, there is raw sewage. It would be above the domestic water intake for the municipalities in that area.
I am glad to know the minister is coming down to that area. Seeing is believing, and we would welcome him there to see at first hand this problem and other conditions.

Mr. Chairman, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not say something pertaining to this problem, which has been discussed so well by the hon. members for Lincoln and Welland. There can be no doubt that a most hazardous condition exists at the Homer bridge. So far this year our tourist traffic is up to the extent of about 12 per cent. On the 4th of July week end at Fort Erie, including the four

days from July 1, 125,000 cars crossed over one bridge alone. On the 4th of July there were issued at the Fort Erie bridge alone
12,000	tourist permits.

I am not exaggerating when I say that, especially on a holiday week end-and it will be understood that when the bridge goes up navigation has preference over all other types of traffic-if more than one boat, goes through, or if perhaps there are two or three of them, I have seen with my own eyes motor cars two abreast extending all the way from St. Catharines right through to Niagara Falls, a distance of 10 miles, waiting for the bridge to go down.
I suggest to the minister that perhaps the most economical and surely the quickest way ;o relieve the situation would be to build a tunnel under the canal, as was suggested by the hon. member for Lincoln. This could be done easily in the winter months, and in a comparatively short time. I hope relief will be given to us in this matter. As the hon. member for Welland said, I hope the minister will give some relief to the municipalities bordering the Welland canal in connection with the services they have to render for the canal itself. Therefore I join.with the other hon. members who have extended an invitation to the minister to visit this district. Let me tell him we will afford him a welcome, with open arms, into God's given country in this great dominion.

Of course, Mr. Chairman, I had always thought that God's country was in the province of Quebec; but I see that perhaps I may have to amend my ideas on the subject. ,
The three hon. members who have just spoken have from time to time since the opening of the session made representations to me personally about these subjects. May I ask the minister the present whereabouts of the Walter E. Foster?
I am sure the hon. member will be gratified to hear that the Walter E. Foster is back in service in the Saint John agency. She is at present at Charlottetown.
I should like to say a few words with respect to that. I could quite easily get worked up over this matter of the Walter E. Foster, but it is a warm day and late in the session.
That applies to both sides of the chamber.

I hope the minister does not mean that he is going to get worked up over me. The Walter E. Foster has a history which has been brought to the attention of the house only through questions and answers and I should like to take a minute to review the situation as it applies to us in the bay of Fundy, particularly at Saint John. Two or three years ago it was decided to build the Walter E. Foster and to all intents and purposes this vessel was to be assigned to Saint John and the bay of Fundy. I looked up the estimates of two years ago and Saint John was definitely there in brackets behind the name Walter E. Foster when the original amount was apportioned for its construction. I attended a very nice ceremony in Montreal last October when I met the Minister of Transport.	.
We were very proud of the Walter E. Foster, which bears the name of a former premier of our province. On completion this fine ship was sent down to the bay of Fundy and was stationed at Saint John. Announcements were made in the paper and there was the usual fanfare given to these things. It was said that the vessel would be on duty in the bay of Fundy. I have looked up the statements made at that time.
In the last few months there was an accident in the gulf of St. Lawrence which made it necessary to provide a replacement for the Lady Grey and it was felt necessary to divert the Walter E. Foster from the bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence. We did not object particularly although we felt that other arrangements could have been made. But if there was urgent need for the Walter E. Foster in

the St. Lawrence we were willing to play our part in things that were immediate.
However, questions were asked-this is the first instance of discrimination-and we did not like the replies the minister gave that it was just not convenient to consider other sources with respect to the servicing of the lightships and icebreaking facilities in the St. Lawrence. We were told later that the vessel would return after the ice season was over. Those statements are on record in this House of Commons. When the vessel did not return at the end of the season I asked a further question with respect to the then whereabouts of the Walter E. Foster. I was told that it was back at Vickers, or back at the shipyards for further repairs.
For repair.

For repairs. That brings out a whole new field as to why repairs are necessary to a new boat. It also brings up the answers to my questions which very comprehensibly inquired as to the condition of the ship, whether changes were necessary, etc. It was stated that they were definitely not needed. However, the vessel is now in Charlottetown, and I am wondering what is the present intention. First of all, if I can just review the situation in chronological order, it was moved from the Bay of Fundy, its base at Saint John, to the St. Lawrence for urgent needs. It was said it would be returned at the end of the ice season. When it was not returned, we inquired further and we were told that it was in the shipyards for repair and it would possibly be sent back on July 15. It is now past July 15. We still have not seen the Foster down our way, and today we are informed it is in Charlottetown.
I want to make this point clear. Is the Walter E. Foster a ship that is destined for Saint John and the bay of Fundy, as it was slated to be, and as was announced to the press with the usual fanfare, or is the Foster to go somewhere else? Are we not to see it again? Has another vessel taken its place? What is the complete story on it? I would appreciate a statement from the minister with respect to the further plans of the Foster. I would also remind him before he replies that we do not object to its temporary move, but we object to the loose way in which the words were used and the way things were postponed from day to day and no definite word was given, because we seemed to be a little far out of the way in the bay of Fundy. Why are the repairs necessary, and where is it going in the future?

Mr. Chairman, I think I should preface my remarks by saying it has never been the policy of the department that, when
Supply-Transport
a vessel is assigned to a particular marine agency, it is an irrevocable and permanent assignment and can under no circumstances be used for other purposes or elsewhere. That must, of course, apply to the Walter E. Foster in the same way as it applies to other vessels.
The difficulty that arose last winter was an outcome of the collision between the Levis ferry and the Lady Grey, resulting in the loss of the Lady Grey. The department was then faced with the question of what vessel could be used to render the services which had to be rendered in the St. Lawrence and which formerly had been given by the icebreaker Lady Grey. The choice was limited. The Franklin, which was in the Saint John agency, was not strengthened for icebreaking and therefore was not serviceable, whereas the Walter E. Foster was.
The hon. member said he had no objection to its being used. I think I told him earlier in the session that when the icebreaking season came to an end the vessel would return to the Saint John agency. Well, at the end of the icebreaking season it was found necessary to have the Foster engine and propeller shaft checked up by the shipbuilders, Vickers, and the ship was sent to Montreal for that purpose. At the moment it is in Charlottetown helping in the Charlottetown agency, but it is our intention to return it to the Saint John agency as soon as possible. So far as next winter is concerned, I should say quite candidly to the hon. member that it is our intention that the Foster shall again take part in the service in the St. Lawrence river. We have no other ship that can be used in her place, and consequently it will be necessary to make use of her for that purpose. The Saint John agency will not be any worse off than in the past. The Franklin is still to be kept in condition. I am not comparing the Franklin with the Foster. The Franklin cannot perform in the St. Lawrence the services we expect of the Foster. I think that covers the matter. I am sorry that they may not be agreeable to the hon. member, but unfortunately those are the facts.

I should like to take a further minute to point out one thing. It was felt necessary at one time to build a new ship for service in the bay of Fundy. It was admitted that the Franklin was old, and the Foster was decided upon. It was in statements made at the launching and in statements made in the newspapers with reference to the naming of the ship after one of our premiers that it was said that the ship should bear the name Walter E. Foster and should be stationed in the bay of Fundy for lightship permanent duty. Credit was given to the government. As I say, they had their

Supply-Transport
usual advertising and fanfare with respect to it. There was a picture in the newspaper, and announcements were made. I do not think it is fair that this ship should be taken away unless there is another emergency situation. If that is the case, then we should have a definite announcement that another ship is being built to take care of the permanent duty in the bay of Fundy.

I hoped I had made it clear the Foster was intended to replace the Franklin and, had we not lost the Lady Grey, I take it the replacement would have been to the satisfaction of the hon. member. Unfortunately, the Lady Grey was lost last year and it is not possible, it has not been possible, and it will not be possible, to replace the Lady Grey for the next icebreaking season. There is the emergency of having to take care of the icebreaking duties, for which the Foster is suitable whereas the Franklin is not. I am afraid the hon. member will have to be satisfied that there is an emergency in the broad sense which makes it necessary to use the Foster in the St. Lawrence. As soon as the emergency has been cured, we expect to return the Foster to the bay of Fundy and replace the Franklin in that way.
In that respect, may I ask the minister what is being done about this emergency?

I said yesterday that plans were being made for the replacement of the Lady Grey. I cannot remember what I said about calling for tenders, but we hope to get on with it as quickly as possible. It is not being delayed.

As a preliminary I would ask the minister whether he would comment on the union situation in so far as ships are concerned; and specifically I would ask him what association there is between the department and the Seafarers' International Union in so far as these employees are concerned?

My information is that on the west coast we have officers who belong to the officers' guild. On both the east and the west coast we have engineers who belong to the Association of Marine Engineers. Then we have seamen who belong to a new association the name of which I do not have at the present time but which is associated with the Civil Service Association. At Halifax and Saint John we have some seamen who

belong to the Seafarers' International Union. That is the extent of my information on the subject.

think perhaps I can up-date the minister a little bit. According to my information, the situation is this. The seamen's union, to which he refers and of which he said he had not the name, is the association of government seafarers, wharf and yard employees, and is usually referred to by its initials. That is a union whose members are governed by civil service regulations and, in so far as that is concerned, I think would follow normal government practice with various employees. However, what the minister apparently is not aware of is that there is a direct affiliation between the A.G.S.W.Y.E.-which are the initials of this union-and the Seafarers' International Union. I quote from the Financial Post of December 4, 1954:
Canada's waterfront baron, Hal C. Banks, this week moved his union activities on board government ships.
Banks' 8,000-member Seafarers' International Union has formed a "working alliance" with the recently established association of government seafarers, wharf and yard employees. The association is a group of government employees, which claims to represent at least 500 seamen and workers on government ships and in federal-operated marine yards.
Then later on we find this:
Banks says that both unions will continue operating as before, with members of the A.G.S.W.Y.E. paying 40 cents on monthly dues to the S.I.U.
And later again:
The new allegiance was effected by the granting of a charter, which brings the A.G.S.W.Y.E. under the jurisdiction of the Seafarers' International Union, which has headquarters in San Francisco. It's understood the two unions will act together on a wide range of matters, including contract negotiations and maritime transportation legislation.
A certain amount of additional information is given but I think what I have quoted establishes the facts with reasonable certainty. To me, Mr. Chairman, this is an arrangement which is unsatisfactory, to say the very least. I have great respect for the work being done by the major labour unions in this country; I refer to the respectable labour unions. I may say that the great majority of them fall into that class. Again I have great respect for most of the leaders of the labour movement, many of whom are my own personal friends. But when I come to the Seafarers' International Union and its leader, I have no respect whatever-
And there are a great many others too.

-for
the labour racketeer who heads that union. The situation has been covered in article 50433-413
Supply-Transport
after article in Maclean's magazine, the Financial Post and various other publications. I will just quote here briefly in order to establish the position of Mr. Banks in so far as the Seafarers' International Union is concerned because apparently we are now going to be dealing to some extent, as a government, with Mr. Banks. We have here the Financial Post of October 16, 1954, which says this:
Many will find the facts of the present sailor union set-up in Canada hair-raising and hardly believable. Many who think all unionism is swathed in idealism and devoted only to do-goodery will be startled.
Today, a man named Harold Chamberlain Banks from a luxurious office on Montreal's St. James street is dictator over some 8,000 men who handle virtually every inland and deep sea ship under Canadian registry.
It is apparent that since that day he has begun to add, directly or indirectly, the government ships. As I have said, unions as such have contributed tremendously to our Canadian economy. We respect them. We admire them. We need them. But a union or any group in the hands of the wrong people can be turned to devious ends.
What is Banks? I have previously referred to him as a labour racketeer. I now refer to him in some detail as a man who has been convicted of certain crimes in Canada; a man who has had certain convictions-one of them carrying 14 years-in the United States; a man who, among other things, has been charged-although I do not suggest he was convicted-with the possession of firearms, murder and child stealing. Incidentally it is rather amusing that in the article which sets out these various aspects of Mr. Banks, the writer says this:
When I mentioned this generally to Mr. Banks, he said something to the effect that most of it stemmed from his long labours on behalf of trade unionism.
When I think of men like Claude Jodoin, Roger Provost, Percy Bengough and the many hundreds of others who have managed to lead labour movements in this country throughout their generation without having attached to them the opprobrium which attaches to this particular man Banks, I question whether these various escapades of his had anything to do with his work for the labour movement. Also, in so far as he is concerned, this seamen's dictator has never even been elected to office. He was sent up here from the United States to do a job which was done quite well, namely that of cleaning out communists out of the Canadian seamen's union. But since that date he has retained power here, in certain ways which I will not describe here, without in any way being elected to office.
This, Mr. Chairman, is the man who now has moved to take over and control the

Supply-Transport
union representing those seamen employed in our government ships or at least those seamen employed in some of our government ships. It can well be expected that, proceeding from these first inroads, he will advance his tactics and further his interests on vessels belonging to the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Public Works. They all operate vessels and they all employ seamen.
I am very surprised that the minister was not aware of this situation, that he has not seen this particular development approaching and that his officials have not advised him of it so that steps might be taken to counteract it. Now that the matter has been brought to his attention I urgently suggest that he take whatever steps are necessary to protect the interests of the government and the seamen, because in the final analysis the seamen gain nothing from association with such an individual as this man. Steps should be taken to remove the seamen's union, which has associations with the Department of Transport, from the control of such an unsuitable individual.

speechtext: May I make these remarks in case the discussion should go further.
