Possibly I did wander a bit outside the rules, Mr. Chairman. However, to conclude, this man has some say in who is employed by the federal government on our ships.
I do not think that statement will bear examination.
I am speaking with that understanding.

I think I should say right away that it has no relation to the facts so far as the Department of Transport is concerned. It is the policy of the department to allow the employees on its ships to belong to a union of their choice. They make the choice, and the department does not interfere with the choice they make. Regardless of the personal opinions one may have with respect to the direction of various labour organizations, I do not see how the department can properly take the attitude of dictating to its employees the union to which they belong.
I am not suggesting any dictation of labour by government. I am stating facts.

I shall conclude by suggesting there should be an investigation by the Department of Labour, and by the Department of National Revenue as to the personal funds that Mr. Banks accumulates, in order to protect our seamen, the best interests of this country and the good name of organized labour.

In the details of this vote on page 563 there is an amount of $2,000 for vocational training for merchant seamen. 1 notice that in the annual report for the year ending March 31, 1954, at page 77, it says the whole program has been completed with the exception of two seamen who have been ill and unable to go ahead with their training. What is the actual situation at the moment? Have there been additional merchant seamen given eligibility for this training?

My note indicates that this amount of $2,000 is for the training of Canadian merchant seamen under the authority of an order in council passed in 1949, and the amount is specifically to provide for four merchant seamen who were granted deferment on medical grounds but who should be fit for training during 1955-56.

I notice the vote for subsidies for salvage companies-I think there are only two of them-has been increased from $80,000 to $150,000. This means that these payments have been almost doubled. Will the minister tell the house what companies will receive these subsidies and why there has been this increase?

I think I must explain that the increase in cost is attributable directly to the increased costs of those who have agreed to provide this stand-by service, which perhaps does not surprise the hon. member. I understand that the contracts had been running for some time. There are two items included in this sum of $150,000, and the moneys will be for the purpose of subsidizing two salvage companies, one at Montreal and one at Vancouver, B.C. This is to ensure that sufficiently efficient plants are maintained to render prompt, effective aid to vessels in distress in the St. Lawrence river and on the coasts of Canada. The amounts are divided equally between Foundation Maritime Limited, Montreal and Pacific Salvage Company Limited, North Vancouver.

Why was there such an
increase?

Perhaps I should point out that it has been represented to the department that the availability of these salvage facilities has had a favourable effect on insurance rates for ships.

There were many people in the west who were disturbed when a member from Montreal became Minister of Transport, because they feared this route would not get its fair share of the nation's business. I might say, however, that the directors were quite pleased with their first interview with the Minister of Transport. Could the minister indicate the volume of business expected through the port at Churchill? How many cargoes are likely to move through there, and when is the navigation season opening? Could he also indicate the stage reached in the construction of the addition to the elevator, and whether there will be a sizeable amount of inward freight handled through the Hudson bay route this year?

I understand there were certain people even in Montreal who were disquieted by the fact that I became Minister of Transport. But it seemed in November last that there were more people who favoured my continuing than those who opposed it.
In Montreal.

I received a delegation representing the Hudson Bay association. We had a most agreeable discussion, during which I told them I thought the traffic into Hudson bay in 1955 would probably be greater than it was in 1954. Last year I believe there were either 35 or 36 ships, and I have been told it is quite likely there will be a greater number in the current season.
Perhaps I might add that the C. D. Howe which we have been discussing during part of this day has already reached the port of Churchill. No freight vessels have yet arrived at that point. However, I believe this year promises to be a better one. There has been an extension of the period recognized by the insurers. This extension involves five or six extra days at the end of

Supply-Transport
the season, which means that the season is thereby prolonged. We are having a greater ice patrol this year and we hope to get more complete reports regarding ice conditions from the civil aviation operators. Ice has been one of the handicaps confronting ships operating into Hudson bay.
What stage has the addition to the elevator reached?
Perhaps we might deal with that when we are on the item for the national harbours board.

I was delighted to hear about the considerable improvement in the use of the facilities of the port of Churchill last year. We do not have any great opportunity in the house to discuss the Hudson Bay Railway and the situation at Fort Churchill. Perhaps this is one occasion when we might be given some up to date information concerning activities there in the past year. In my view the part played by the Hudson bay route in future will be just as important to the mid-continent region as that of the St. Lawrence seaway, when it is completed. I was impressed particularly by the extension of the minimum insurance rate for a further period.
Of five or six days.

Yes, five or six days. That has been a steady process down through the years; and there is no reason why, with improved navigational facilities and broadening experience, there should not be a continual lengthening of the minimum rate period.
There is one question in connection with the Hudson Bay Railway I would like the minister to answer. One of the outstanding annual tourist events in Manitoba is the excursion to Churchill. Citizens in local towns along the route turn out with bands playing to give a special welcome to those taking part in the excursion. I believe, however, that it is an event which takes place only once each year. As it is a popular tourist attraction in that part of the country, I have been wondering if there is any possibility of its being held more frequently. Would the minister indicate the intentions of the department in that regard?

I would be pleased to take up the matter with the Canadian National Railways. I am sure they would welcome and carry out any suggestion that would be likely to add to their revenues. If the hon. member believes his suggestion would have that effect, then I have no doubt it would commend itself to the C.N.R. management.

Would the minister be good enough to answer that part of the question
TMr. Marler.]
asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie which dealt with incoming freight along this route? Has the volume been growing or is the reverse true?

I do not believe I need say anything more about exports through Churchill, because I think we all understand that is not a matter which can be settled readily, but I think we all agree that the future of Churchill is going to depend in large measure upon the amount of goods brought in from overseas through that port. I have some figures here which I find a little difficult to summarize, but I think I should say that the volume of imports is not really very impressive. According to my figures, last year there were 110 carloads representing a total of 2,131 tons. I think we must agree that this does not represent a very substantial amount.
One gentleman from England who visited me some weeks ago told me that he was hopeful of bringing in some British cargoes. It may well be that these figures should be looked upon as being something of the past, and that there will be a substantial improvement in the future. I suppose a good deal will depend upon how persuasive consignees in western Canada are in getting shippers in the United Kingdom and elsewhere to send their cargoes through Churchill. I am sure the hon. member realizes that there are a large number of factors involved, and I do not think there is anything I could do personally that would add to or subtract from the total volume. Perhaps the hon. member would be interested to learn that the two commodities which seem to stand out rather prominently are glass and whisky.

Have the officers of the department made a survey for a route that would run up into the interlake country through Hodgson and then join the Hudson Bay Railway? I referred to this many years ago in the house.
I am afraid I do not understand where we are going to or coming from.

From Hodgson straight north to meet the Hudson Bay Railway. I just forget how many miles could be saved. I understand there would be only one expensive bridge to be built, and it would provide a direct outlet to this Manitoba seaport. With modern instruments it may be possible to get into Hudson bay before the C. D. Howe got there this year, and leave at a much later time.
We would be better off if the ice did not get there first.

Item agreed to.

472. Construction of new dock and terminal facilities at Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, $650,000.

This item has to do with the construction of a new dock and terminal facilities at Port aux Basques. The minister wall remember that yesterday I asked why work of this kind should not be done by the Department of Public Works rather than the Department of Transport. Could the minister give us an answer to that question?

I think one of the handicaps under which a newly arrived minister suffers is that he has no information as to why decisions were taken originally. I know this matter was referred to a couple of days ago. The only reason I can think of is that as the facilities are to be entrusted to the Canadian National Railways for operation and management, the construction was carried out by the Department of Transport in collaboration with Canadian National Railways.

There must be some basis on which the government decides that the Department of Public Works will build a dock in one city and the Department of Transport will build a similar structure in another city. As the minister knows, most of the docks in Canada have been built by the Department of Public Works but here is a case where the Department of Transport stepped in and presumably pushed out the Department of Public Works.
I do not think so.

Does it not mean that there is a duplication as far as the Department of Transport is concerned? If that department is going to build docks it will have to have engineers and other experts. The Department af Public Works already has experts of that type. Why should construction of this kind not be entrusted to the Department of Public Works?

I am afraid I cannot give an answer other than that I gave a moment ago. I should like the hon. member to understand that in this particular case we are not building up a staff in the Department of Transport to build docks and wharves. The engineering in connection with this project was done by outside consulting engineers, as I think was the case in connection with the dock and facilities at North Sydney, Nova Scotia. I am told there have been other cases in the past where ferry services were concerned where the work was carried out under the direction of this department rather than the Department of Public Works.
Supply-Transport
Instead of turning this work over to the Department of Public Works the Department of Transport actually hired outside engineers to do the work?
Just as the Department of Public Works did at North Sydney.

I think the minister should explain a little more fully just how this work at Port aux Basques was carried out. On July 19 I questioned the Minister of Public Works about this, and I quote from page 6405 of Hansard beginning with a question which I asked:
Why were there not preliminary surveys?
Preliminary surveys of what?

Of the whole project. Why was it not planned in advance? A child would understand that a ship would have to be of such a size that it could be operated into this harbour. Surely the master mariners knew very well, and have known all along, what was necessary in order to operate a ship in that harbour. We read that the Newfoundland press and the people of Newfoundland have been warning the government for months or even for years that there would be this fiasco. Why were there not preliminary plans made so that this result could have been avoided?

Why don't you ask the Minister of Transport if there were?
I am following the advice of the Minister of Public Works and asking the Minister of Transport.

Mr. Chairman, to imply that no planning was done is not in accordance with the facts. The planning was done, as I understand it, by Mr. McCulloch, the consulting engineer for the terminal facilities, the dock and sheds. The design of the terminal and their location were agreed upon in collaboration with the Canadian National Railways. I understand that the location of the channel which was dredged by the Department of Public Works was at the suggestion of the Canadian National Railways or of our engineer. I have endeavoured to clear up that point. I have not been able to do so. I do not think it is material. The channel obviously was placed in the position it now occupies so as to provide a straight run into the terminal and a run out from the terminal to the sea. The extent of the dredging was relatively minor.
As I said yesterday during my remarks on the subject, most of the dredging that was done was of material that lay between depths of 10 feet and 23 feet. It has been suggested in some articles I have seen that a whole island was removed. Nothing could be further from the truth. The channel I am speaking of lies between Pike's island on the east and Vardy's island on the west. Personally I cannot bring myself to believe, though I lay no claim to being an expert, that the removal of 18,000 cubic yards of material from the

Supply-Transport
shoals which lay between the two islands did have the dreadful effect that seems to have been attributed to it by some of these newspaper articles.
As I said yesterday, the question of the depth of the channel also has been given a significance which I think is not in line with the facts. I made some such answer as that to the hon. member for Greenwood. The depth of the channel at the lowest stage of water at any time in the year is 23 feet, and the draft of the vessel fully loaded, which I suppose would happen not regularly but from time to time, is 19 feet 3 inches. It seems to me there is adequate clearance for the vessel. A difficulty which seems to have arisen-and personally I find it hard to believe that it could have been anticipated beforehand-is that the wind and wave actions at the terminal is considered to present possible dangers if the ship enters in calm weather and a very severe storm blows up from the southeast or southwest.
The difficulty may arise from the fact that the loading facilities do not admit of a great deal of movement of the ship at the dock. As I said yesterday, the ferry William Carson has been entrusted to Canadian National Railways for operation. Some of their senior officials have doubts whether the safety of the vessel may not be compromised if, while it is moored at the terminal, a severe storm should blow up and the effect of wind and wave surge at the terminal necessitate the movement of the ship. Without having any personal views whatever as to the technical aspects of the question, I feel that as the management of the C.N.R. is to have the responsibility for the safety of the ship, we must pay a great deal of attention to their views in connection with the operation of the vessel. They fear that this condition may arise.
On the other hand there are other people- not charged, I admit, with responsibility for the safety of the ship-who consider that the ship could operate into the terminals as they are now. In the face of this doubt we have had a number of conferences with the senior officers and engineering officials of the railways and the Department of Public Works to see if it was not possible to reconcile the conflicting views. Some people thought it would be desirable to provide further protection in the harbour. There are others who consider that further protection is not necessary. Some believe that protection should be placed further in, and some believe it should be placed further out.
Under these circumstances it seemed to us -and we had the opportunity of discussing

the matter earlier this week-that we should seek to obtain the services of an independent and competent expert who would have no attachment to the Canadian National Railways, to the Department of Public Works or to my own department, and who would give us an objective view on the present situation. On Tuesday I initiated some efforts in that direction which have not yet produced any result, but I am hopeful that either this week or next it will be possible for us in the Department of Transport to retain the services of a disinterested third party, an engineer of outstanding capability, who will tell us if further works are required in order to make the harbour of Port aux Basques safe for operating the Carson under all kinds of what I might call reasonable weather. We are not talking about calm days but, on the other hand, we are not talking either about hurricanes. I think it will be possible to get such an expert to work at once, so we can be told objectively and in a way that ought to be acceptable to all concerned whether or not further works are required and the extent of those further works.
I have tried to take an entirely objective view of the situation, as hon. members know, with regard to the construction of these facilities in Port aux Basques. The dredging took place before I became minister. Apart from any responsibilities I have inherited I do not think that I have had any other responsibilities in connection with the matter.
I cannot help thinking we have a choice of two positions: Either that the situation that now exists is safe despite the fears expressed by the senior officials of the Canadian National Railways, or that the harbour is such that further protection was necessary from the moment Canada undertook as part of the terms of union to provide a ferry service of the dimensions to which I alluded yesterday in my remarks.
An important factor to bear in mind is that this is not just a matter of replacing smaller vessels that have been used and are being used for passenger service to Port aux Basques now. It is a matter of providing a new form of service with a vessel that is capable of carrying passengers and freight. I am quite sure it is not necessary to stress the point, but in order to have a ship that is capable of rendering the service with such frequency, arriving one morning at Port aux Basques, leaving that evening for North Sydney and continuing the cycle the following day, it is very important that we should have a ship that is capable of operating in all conditions of weather, that will load and unload quickly and that will have the power that is necessary to operate particularly in

bad winter weather. I think that calls for the kind of ship the William Carson is.
I must say I am very unhappy over the fact that the service has not started right away. But I said yesterday that the matter had only recently been brought to my attention, and that is no exaggeration of the facts. We are hopeful that it will be possible to clear up the situation very quickly. I do not know just what work we shall have to do. Shall we have to do any further work? I am afraid I cannot answer that question either. As I said yesterday, Canada is committed to providing this ferry service and we are going to carry out that commitment. We are going to do whatever is required in order to meet that commitment.

The minister has not explained what department did the planning for the ship. Someone, somewhere, designed the ship. I am wondering whether that was exclusively the responsibility of the Department of Transport or whether the Canadian National Railways assumed that responsibility, or whether both those bodies were responsible.

I understand that the Canadian maritime commission, the Canadian National Railways and the department had a committee which considered the whole question of the construction of the ferry and the character of the vessel that ought to be provided.
When was this planning commenced?
In 1950, I believe.

Then, Mr. Chairman, we have this picture. The Department of Transport, the Canadian maritime commission and the Canadian National Railways planned this ship. They worked out the size of it and all the particulars about using elevators to help in the speedy discharge of the freight.
If I might interject for a moment, I should like to say that part was done by the Canadian National Railways.
That was done by the Canadian National Railways?
Yes.
But apparently the Department of Transport was involved in the decision as to the size of the ship.
I think so; yes.

Then the Department of Transport and the Canadian National Railways decided what dredging would be done in the harbour. Is that correct?
Supply-Transport

Mr. Chairman, I find it difficult to answer that question categorically because I have not been able personally to find out whether it was decided by the Canadian National Railways or by the department. I am quite sure my hon. friend will understand my difficulty. The engineer of the department, Mr. Moore, who was directly concerned with those operations, died some months ago. He could have told us the answers to these questions, but I am afraid I cannot answer for him.
From what the Minister of Public Works said the other day it seems that the Department of Public Works had nothing whatever to do with the planning of the dredging. Is that correct?
I think that is so.

As reported at page 6405 of Hansard he said this:
On the part of the work for which we are responsible surveys were made. I am just a contractor for this part of the work. The Department of Transport said, "Will you dig a channel on this centre line?" We dug a channel on the centre line, after making adequate surveys.
I think that is correct.
By the way, I think that the minister said they hired a consultant to advise on this harbour development.

I hope, Mr. Chairman, I did not give the impression that Mr. McCulloch had the responsibility for dredging, because that was not by intention. Mr. McCulloch acted as consulting engineer in connection with the terminal facilities, but not in connection with the dredging. As my colleague the Minister of Public Works said, his department acted as agent for us and not on its own.
In addition to the dredging, someone decided that the dock would be moved to a new site. The minister said yesterday-
I do not think I said "moved". I think I said "would be built".

Yes. I think the minister said that a dock would be built on a new site. As reported at page 6467 of Hansard he said:
The second is that the new terminal is located upon a site not previously used as a wharf and there was no earlier experience that would serve to establish what effect wind and wave used to have on that part of the harbour.
Yes.
Who made that decision? Was it the Canadian National Railways or was it the Department of Transport?
I understand that decision was taken by the Canadian National Railways.
Supply-Transport

The work was done. The ship was built. The country spent $21,760,000. Then after a period of four or five years, when the ship is ready to operate, we find that the Canadian National Railways officials now say that the harbour is not safe for the ship. The minister intimates that there is some doubt whether that is an accurate statement, or whether the Canadian National officials are right.
Yes, that is right.

But they apparently have now taken the position that the harbour is not satisfactory for the ship and that the ship cannot be operated into the harbour with safety. Surely that is not just a matter to shrug off and say, "Oh, well, it is just too bad; we now find that the ship we built cannot use the harbour safely and we are obliged to do something now to remedy the situation". Does the minister not think this was a big mistake on somebody's part? Either in his department or in the Canadian National Railways there has been a gross blunder. Either there has been carelessness or inefficiency in making the plans in the first place, or something wrong has been done either in the Department of Transport or the Canadian National Railways. In either case the responsibility comes back to the minister.
I agree at once that personally it is not this minister's responsibility, because he has been in the portfolio for only about a year. But here is a mistake-a very big and bad mistake-in the department under his direction.
I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member but I wonder if he would permit me to ask this question. Would the hon. member tell me what he considers to be the mistake?

I think the mistake is this. You have spent $21,760,000. You have a brand new ship on your hands, you have a new dock and you have a harbour, with some cost for the dredging, which is two feet too shallow.
No.
The dredging is not deep enough.
No.

Or you dredged in the wrong places, and you cannot use this ship in the harbour. If that is not a mistake I do not know what is. The very facts speak for themselves.
I think the minister would have been wiser to come into the house and admit quite frankly that there has been a mistake in his department and say, "We are sorry; we will see that this sort of thing does not happen again". I believe this situation calls for fairly

drastic action either in the Department of Transport or in the Canadian National Railways; and I am extremely doubtful whether the blame can be attached to the Canadian National Railways. I think the minister's own department should take the blame, and that steps should be taken to see that this sort of thing does not happen again.
We are building these extremely expensive vessels and we shall be building more of them all the time. Today we had a vote for a new ship to cost $81 million. Somebody in the department or in some branch should have a going-over. I hope the minister will not be content just to say, "Nobody is to blame. It is just too bad. Now we will start again". I do not think that is good enough. I do not think that is a satisfactory way in which to meet a situation of this kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I want to ask one question. Perhaps I have a special interest in this matter because I have been at Port aux Basques a good many times and the problem comes very vividly to me on that account. There is one thing that strikes me forcibly. We have had three departments here putting their heads together. I suppose it is almost a case of too many cooks. The question I want to ask is this. We have the Department of Public Works which does various kinds of work. We have the Department of Transport. Then we have the Canadian National Railways which seems, almost by the rub of the green here, to have had an especially heavy responsibility. One is struck with the fact that what was wanted was a straight run. That phrase seems to have been in everybody's mind. It almost sounds more like a railway than a ship channel. I want to ask this question. You had these three departments-
Two departments.

Two departments; we will count one out-and you had this job which primarily, as I see it, among other things needed a harbour engineer of the highest quality. There are such. In Europe particularly I know that harbour engineering is a very highly specialized art, a very complicated and difficult one. Was there anyone in this situation who, at the time the plans were made, could be regarded as a highly qualified harbour engineer? If there was not it seems to me obvious that, if that was omitted, the greatest and most obvious point of all was simply not dealt with.
I think Mr. McCulloch unquestionably is a qualified engineer so far as terminal facilities are concerned.
When did he come into the picture?
He came in at the very beginning, when the terminal facilities were being built. As I said a moment ago, I want to make it perfectly clear that' Mr. McCulloch has no responsibility for the dredging.
For what?
For the dredging.

I want to make it perfectly clear that Mr. McCulloch was consulted with respect to the building of the terminal facilities both at Port aux Basques and North Sydney, and I want to make it perfectly clear that he did not have any responsibility for the dredging.
May I ask-

Perhaps the hon. member might let me finish. I think Mr. Moore of my department, either with or without consultation with Canadian National Railways because I cannot determine that from any records, was responsible for the determination of the location of the channel.
Including the dredging?

Well, I am not suggesting he was responsible for the actual dredging, because that was carried out by the Department of Public Works. But the Department of Public Works carried it out as the agent of the Department of Transport, and I do not think anybody would suggest it had not been done as expected, or was not well done.
Was Mr. Moore a harbour engineer?
He was a general engineer in my department until his death last December.
Would I be correct in inferring that he was not a harbour engineer in a highly specialized sense?
I think that would be a correct inference.
Then we come back to Mr. McCulloch. Was he a harbour engineer of high qualifications?
I think so, yes.

But apparently he was not' asked this question. As I understand it, he determined where the terminal was to be built, but the minister was frank to say that this harbour engineer, apparently a highly qualified harbour engineer, was not asked his opinion on this most difficult question and had no responsibility for what was done. Is that correct?

I think so, yes.
50433-ilii
Supply-Transport

There is no point in pursuing the matter with the minister because, as we all recognize, he was not there at the time. But I cannot help saying that it seems to me this is a fair summary of the situation. You had a most difficult task of harbour engineering, and I can quite believe it was a difficult task, and you had a harbour engineer of apparently high qualifications, but was he asked to give his opinion on the harbour engineering? No, this harbour engineer was not asked his opinion and, so far as I understand the situation, no highly qualified harbour engineer was employed to make this decision which I should have thought was a very difficult, important and indeed vital decision affecting the whole enterprise.

I have already make it clear that I think Mr. McCulloch has no professional responsibility for the channel or for the dredging. Perhaps I should add that in connection with the channel the late Mr. Moore of my department held a number of meetings at Port aux Basques at which Mr. McCulloch was present. I understand the whole subject of the location of the channel was discussed orally. Unfortunately, as I said earlier, I cannot tell members of the committee what took place because I had no conversations with Mr. Moore before his death, and the fact of his death makes it impossible for us to know what took place at these meetings and what was said.
I should like to conclude my own comments by saying that I readily understand that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra would like to put me in the position of rendering judgment in this situation. I am not going to render judgment. I think it is a highly technical question and I would prefer to wait until we have the review of the situation made by the expert to whom I referred a moment ago. If he says that what has been done was a mistake I shall be prepared to admit it, but I do not propose to do so beforehand. I shall wait until I hear what his judgment of the situation is before I confess judgment in the matter.
The minister said yesterday and he has repeated today that he intends to hire an independent expert to find out whether a mistake was made.
Not whether a mistake was made; whether or not further protective works are necessary.

Is there no staff in the Department of Transport, the Department of Public Works or the national harbours board competent to advise the government on this question?

Supply-Transport

Mr. Chairman, I think there are competent persons, but I know what my hon. friend or others in the opposition would say if we were to choose people in the government service. They would say we had merely got somebody to bless the present situation and no matter what was said it would be wrong. I am going to take the precaution of having somebody who will be entirely independent, who is not connected with the C.N.R., the Department of Transport or the Department of Public Works, and who will render an unfettered, free judgment on the situation.
The minister did not answer my question. I asked him whether there are competent men-
I thought I answered that question at the beginning.
-in the Department of Transport, including the national harbours board, or in the Department of Public Works who can deal with this situation?

That was the very first thing I said, but I will repeat that I think there are competent people in the Department of Public Works, I think there are competent people in the national harbours board and I think there are competent people in the agencies of the Department of Transport. However, I prefer to have someone who will not be labelled afterward as having whitewashed everything that was done in connection with Port aux Basques.

Item agreed to.
473. To provide for the payment during the fiscal year 1955-56 to the Canadian National Railway Company (hereinafter called the national company) upon applications approved by the Minister of Transport made from time to time by the national company to the Minister of Finance and to be applied by the national company in the payment of the deficit (certified by the auditors of the national company) in the operation of the North Sydney, Nova Scotia-Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, ferry and terminals arising in the calendar year 1955, $2,350,000.

This item has to do with the C.N.R., and I have been advised of one practice which apparently is being followed. I merely draw it to the minister's attention in the hope that he can do something about it. Apparently a person in the United Kingdom intending to come to Canada on a visit can purchase sleeping car accommodation from the Canadian National Railways office there. But if he is unable to get that accommodation when he comes to Canada, if for any reason it is not available, instead of getting a refund here in Canada he must write to London and get a refund from the London office. It is very inconvenient and 
causes great delay. This, I think, is purely a matter of administration, but I hope the minister will have it checked by someone in his department to see if it cannot be corrected.
I shall be glad to do so.

Item agreed to.
477. Degaussing and strengthening for armament, sea-going merchant ships of Canadian registry of 1,000 gross tons and over, $350,000.
How many ships have been degaussed under this plan?

I think I could say approximately 35 or 40 ships have been covered in the past, that is have been degaussed and stiffened. In the fiscal year 1954-55, some 30 ships were covered, and under the provisions for this year I think there will be 17 ships degaussed and stiffened, one or the other.
Has the minister any idea when this program will be completed? I presume all these ships on both coasts are to be done. Is there any estimate when the work will be completed?
No, I think it is a continuing program, and it applies only to ships of 1,000 tons or over.

Item agreed to.
479. Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited-to provide for the payment from time to time to the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited (hereinafter called "the company") of the amount of the deficit occurring during the year ending December 31, 1955, in the operations of the company and the vessels under the control of the company, as certified by the auditors of the company, and upon applications made by the company to the Minister of Finance and approved by the Minister of Transport, not exceeding, $288,500.

I wonder if the minister would say something pursuant to the question I asked this morning. He and I were present at a meeting of the committee which dealt with the West Indies steamships. I said this morning I was left with a feeling that the attitude was rather lukewarm. A lot of people were not very sure whether it was worth vigorously expanding the business or whether to go slow on it. I have here the last report of the line for 1954, which showed some encouraging signs. Without expecting the minister to go into the subject deeply, I wish he would say a few words about it, perhaps referring particularly to the currency situation. They are a sterling area, are they not? Perhaps he would also say a word as to the trade prospects and the part to be played in that by this shipping line.
I am sorry if the hon. member for Greenwood thinks I feel lukewarm about the matter. I thought during the discussions in the sessional committee-
I am ready to be corrected.

I shall endeavour to correct the hon. member's impression by saying I do not feel lukewarm about it. I think the situation at present is difficult for a number of reasons. The first is that I believe we would all agree that operating it on a year to year basis, without knowing during the year how much longer it is to continue, is not a sound policy. For that reason the government is attempting at the present time to give that kind of consideration to the problem which will enable us to reach a decision as to whether the service ought to be discontinued or ought to be continued for a term long enough to get the best out of the operation.
The second thing I should like to say is that as the hon. member for Greenwood knows, one of the great difficulties in operating to the West Indies is the competition that comes from other ships. We had the case of Saguenay Terminals, which was discussed during the proceedings before the committee. I feel all shipping services operate under highly competitive conditions, and I do not think this one is any exception. As I said this morning, the subject of the continuance of the West Indies service is under study now by an interdepartmental committee. As soon as we receive their report on the matter it will be possible to come to a definite decision as to the future.

Perhaps I might add one comment. I find that the meaning of "lukewarm" is moderately warm, but not zealous; indifferent, so that was the suggestion I made about the minister and he has disclaimed it. It is now four months since we had the meetings of the railway committee, and I think we are entitled to assume the government would have done some thinking on the matter since then. I gather the situation is very much as it was, and I do not thing anything is to be gained by taking a lot of time on it. We will just hope for the best.

I would be the last person to discourage the hon. member from hoping for the best. A very careful economic study of the question has already begun, and we hope to have it completed during this summer. As I said earlier, as soon as the interdepartmental committee have given us their recommendation we will try to come to a decision. I said I was not lukewarm. I suppose if I use the

757. To authorize the governor in council to
grant to the government of the province of British Columbia a subsidy of $25,000 per mile, but not exceeding fifty miles, towards the construction of a line of railway of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway northward from Prince George in the province of British Columbia; such grant of subsidy to be made in such manner and in such amounts and subject to such conditions, if any, as the governor in council deems expedient; estimated requirement for the fiscal year 1955-56, $250,000.

This vote is to provide $250,000 as part of a subsidy to help pay for the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway in British Columbia from Prince George for a distance to the north not exceeding 50 miles.
I believe all the people of British Columbia are very much disappointed that the federal government has drawn the line and said, We will only subsidize for a distance of 50 miles, instead of offering a subsidy for the whole distance from Prince George into the Peace river country. When the Prime Minister announced this subsidy on June 3 he had this to say, and I quote from page 4390:
In regard to the proposed extension northward from Prince George to Fort St. John and Dawson Creek, we doubt that the construction of the whole of this line would be an economic undertaking at this time. It does not appear to us that the potential volume of traffic-
He also said:
Though these considerations lead this government to believe that the through line proposed by British Columbia is not economically justified at this time, we consider that the possibilities for development of the timber resources north of Prince George would justify an extension of up to some 50 miles in that area. We think this would assist materially in the further development of central British Columbia, and that would be to the obvious advantage of the national economy.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that statement is very much out of line with statements that have been made by this same government in the past. I refer the minister, for example, to the report of a special committee on reconstruction and re-establishment, which will be found in Votes and Proceedings for 1943-44 commencing at page 723. I think perhaps this was a joint committee of the house and the Senate, I am not just sure, but in any

Supply-Transport
event it was under Senator Turgeon, who was then in this house. They did a great deal of very useful work and made certain recommendations with regard to transportation, among which was this reference to the railway from Prince George to the Peace river country, as it is found in paragraph 6 of their recommendations:
That the Peace river country of British Columbia and Alberta be given direct railway connection with the Pacific coast at the earliest possible moment. This railway connection is essential to the proper economic development of British Columbia and Alberta; without it, Canada as a nation will lose a great part of the value of the coming exploration and development of the northwest portion of Canada, opened up by military air routes and the Alaska highway.
That report stressed the importance of an outlet. It was not a matter of completing a few miles but rather the matter of an outlet from the Peace river country to the coast. The same question came up again in the second session of 1949 on the introduction of a bill providing for a subsidy for the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway from Quesnel to Prince George. Here I quote from what was said by the present Minister of Fisheries, as it is reported at page 1450 of Hansard for November 4, 1949:
I want to warn hon. members however that when this subsidy of $15,000 a mile-
' The subsidy in that case was $15,000, not $25,000 as proposed here.
-for this construction is passed, I do not think it will be the last time this house will be asked to help in the extension of the P.G.E. Premier Johnson's avowed purpose-
At that time the dominion government was subsidizing a proposal by a coalition government headed by a Liberal premier. I believe that has something to do with the difference in the approach in 1949 and that of today.
Premier Johnson's avowed purpose in connection with that railway is to do what was originally intended; that is, push it through the Rocky mountains into the Peace river block, where there is great traffic in wheat and in the finest anthracite coal in Canada, and where there are also potential oil fields. At the present time the Peace river block of Alberta and British Columbia is served by the Northern Alberta railway; but from the town of Prince George in British Columbia to Dawson Creek at the end of the line, traffic now must travel back to Edmonton for a total of 947 miles. In other words, wheat moving to Prince Rupert has to travel this distance of 947 miles, whereas the actual distance between the two points is only 160 'miles. Completion of the next link between Prince George and Dawson Creek will shorten the rail haul from the Peace river block to the Pacific coast by seme 750 miles. At the present time the provincial government is building a road between Prince George and the Peace river block, but heavy freight such as wheat and coal will never be moved efficiently by truck; it will require a railroad.
Mr. Sinclair went on to say:
I want to just mention this briefly because-

He had given details in an earlier paragraph.
-when we are passing this appropriation 1 think we should be fully aware of all the implications, since we are committing ourselves to a policy of subsidizing the extension of this provincial railway.
The present premier of British Columbia, of course, is not a Liberal. He happens to belong to the Social Credit party. He has asked for a subsidy in connection with building this outlet from the Peace river area to the Pacific coast; but instead of receiving help for the whole line he is told by the Prime Minister that the dominion government will subsidize only for 50 miles, and that it thinks the provincial government has no business to go ahead and extend the line into the Peace river country. The Prime Minister of Canada wished the premier of British Columbia good luck in putting the line through to the Peace river country. He said at page 4391:
We have not yet been able to come to the conclusion that it would bring to the national economy such advantages as would warrant recommending more than we are recommending as an item in the supplementary estimates to be brought down.
As I pointed out a moment ago, the whole purpose of this line is to give the Peace river country an outlet to the Pacific coast. Yet the Prime Minister of Canada is taking the position that there need be only 50 miles built north of Prince George, and that the dominion government will not give any assistance in putting the line right through to the Peace river area. I suggest to the minister that this is unfair treatment, and that the government should keep in mind expenditures such as those on the St. Lawrence seaway and other large projects being developed. I believe the dominion government should express willingness to assist in the construction of the line right through to the Peace river country.
I have nothing more to add at the moment, but I do hope the minister will comment on the fact that they are going to subsidize only for a distance of 50 miles.

When the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra read from the remarks of the Prime Minister he stopped, inappropriately, before dealing with two paragraphs that I think are very important, and which explain the attitude taken by the government. The Prime Minister said, as reported at page 4390:
The principal resources to be developed are the forests north of Prince George. In the mountains to the north of the Parsnip river there are coal deposits which are apt some day to be worth developing, but we are advised that those operating equally good coal deposits in southern British Columbia are now facing economic difficulties due to shrinking markets. Consequently there does not seem to us to be need at this time to carry the

extension northward through the mountains in order to develop coal. The oil and gas on the eastern side of the mountains would, of course, move by pipe line rather than by rail.
The Peace river area itself already has rail access through the Northern Alberta Railways and although this railway taps the greater part of the area it does not obtain a sufficient volume of traffic to result in profitable operations.
Those are two very significant paragraphs; and I think I should also read this further one:
Our view that the present outlook does not justify a further extension of the line at this time would not, of course, prevent consideration of this matter again in a later year if the prospects for economic development then appear to be sufficiently promising to warrant a contribution toward the cost of constructing such an extension at that time.
I think that is very clear. I would repeat what I said this morning, that following the statement by the Prime Minister an official of the British Columbia government came to Ottawa and had discussions with some of our officials here. It was understood that written representations supplying further information would be submitted, and that we would reexamine the question in the light of those written submissions.

Mr. Chairman, I have some observations to make. Would you call it six o'clock?

I wonder if this is the point in the estimates where the minister intended to make a reply to some of the points raised yesterday evening in connection with air services?

Mr. Chairman, last evening the hon. member referred to the policies of the government with regard to civil aviation, and made particular reference to the subject of regional competition. He quoted a passage from an address the Prime Minister had made to the air industries and transport association at Ottawa on October 28, 1953, one paragraph of which was as follows:
As you well know, that decision is apt to have broader implications than merely the settlement of the rival claims of two companies.
Let me assure you that whichever way the decision goes now it will not in the long run be a decision in favour of perpetuation of monopoly conditions. I have stated many times before representatives of other industries that the government to which I belong believes that as a general rule the public can be best served under competitive 
conditions. And I believe that once the air transport industry is soundly established, the decision to be made by any Canadian government should be In favour of opportunities for competition.
And in view of the tremendous development of our resources that has been taking place, a development which shows no sign of relenting, the demands for the services of commercial aircraft should increase to such an extent that increasing competition will be both desirable and beneficial.
I have not taken pains to verify that this is the exact quotation which the hon. member used last evening, but I think it is. 1 think it states faithfully what the Prime Minister said in October, 1953. But I do not think that statement should be detached from an earlier paragraph in the same address which I think is even more enlightening than the paragraph I have just read. I should like to read to the committee that paragraph in the Prime Minister's address which I think perhaps makes clearer than it seemed to be to the hon. member what was the policy of the government and what the Prime Minister had in mind when he spoke to the air industries and transport association in 1953. He said:
The decision that my colleagues and I will make, will have to be made with these two principles in mind: First of all we will try to decide what is best for the public, whether or not from now on the public can be served better by two competing lines, not just for a short period but indefinitely. And secondly, our decision will be based on what will be the best for the industry itself. We will endeavour to determine whether or not there is enough business in sight for two lines to serve the public at reasonable rates and with reasonable profit. Surely it would not be in the interests of either line to permit a situation where both would be forced to operate at a loss for years to come.
The hon. member opposite is very much interested in the case of Associated Airways Limited. If my memory serves me rightly, Associated Airways Limited wished to establish a commercial air service for the transport of goods only, serving Edmonton and Fort McMurray, Alberta; Beaverlodge, Saskatchewan; Fort Smith, Fort Resolution, Yellowknife and Hay River, in the Northwest Territories. This service was to be in competition with Canadian Pacific Air Lines Limited, which operates a passenger and cargo service over the same route. That company opposed the application of Associated Airways Limited, as my hon. friend knows because he represented Associated Airways at the hearings before the air transport board.
As I think he said last night, a hearing of the case took place at Edmonton on July 19 and 20, 1954. As the hon. member said, the air transport board about the middle of October drafted a judgment which I think he would have considered to be favourable to the claims of his client. The draft decision was submitted to me and, after having

examined it, I suggested to the board that they should reconsider their decision. The board did so, and a decision was rendered on November 30, 1954, in which the board denied the application on the ground that the time was not opportune to permit competition to develop between the applicant and the carrier now operating over the route applied for, and that the requirements regarding competition which had been laid down by the government had not been satisfied.
I am sorry to say that I actually confirmed that decision, though I think on rereading the act I ought not to have formed it at that time. Perhaps I might just interrupt the recitation of the facts to say that at the time I confirmed the decision I had not seen the record or the pleadings; I was merely concerned with the formal judgment of the board. As I said a moment ago, I approved it though I think under the act I ought not to have approved it because I think my approval or disapproval was unnecessary.
Associated Airways appealed from this decision to the minister. I should like to tell my hon. friend that the record-I think he will admit it was a voluminous one-was given the most careful study by the permanent officials of my department, and after they had read the record I took the trouble personally to read it from beginning to end and give a great deal of consideration to it. I reached the conclusion personally that the appeal ought to be dismissed, and I may say that was also the view of the permanent officials of my department. The grounds for dismissing the appeal are summarized in the following paragraph:
A review of the evidence on which decision 860 is based discloses that the appellant has failed to establish that the proposed commercial air service is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity or will be in the public interest; on the contrary it appears that if the licence applied for were granted, the operation of the proposed service would prejudice the operation of the services being performed by the intervenant-
That is, Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
-and therefore would not be in the public interest.
The hon. member will remember that the fact that I had approved the initial decision was made a ground by him for an appeal to the cabinet, but I think he must realize that the act contemplated no such procedure and that it was my duty as minister, notwithstanding my previous approval of the formal judgment, to dispose of the appeal. But I assure him that I had not read the record at the time, and it was only when the appeal was before me that I took the trouble to examine every detail of it.

I should like to add one further word in connection with the procedure. After I had come to the conclusion that the act did not contemplate my approval of a negative decision, I advised the chairman of the board that in future I wished the board to come to its decision itself, that it should take the responsibility of making its decisions and that I would take the responsibility of approving or disapproving it. That is the procedure that is contemplated by the act.
I cannot really believe the hon. member would seriously contend that there had been political intervention in that particular case. Certainly nothing could be further from the truth. I might say that a number of hon. members, while the appeal was before me, urged me to maintain the appeal. I felt that on the record there was no other conclusion to come to but that of approval of the decision of the board itself.
Now that was based on the record, but there is something else with which perhaps my hon. friend would not agree. That is, in September and October of last year, when the question was under consideration by the air transport board, we were in a moderate recession in Canada and the question which was uppermost in my mind at that time and which, I feel perfectly convinced, had a great deal of influence on the decision which the board reached was that the time of a decline in the economy was not an opportune moment to initiate competition on a regional basis between these particular points.
That obviously is a matter of opinion. I do not expect the hon. member, who had the interest of his clients to represent, to agree with my contentions, but I hope at least he will attribute to me an endeavour to deal with the matter objectively. I have a very high opinion of his client. I think they are a very excellent company. I think their operations in Canada have been most creditable, and it was a matter of regret in a personal sense that I came to the conclusion that their pretensions were not as well founded as, I am sure, my hon. friend thought they were.
The two paragraphs of the statement made by the Prime Minister in October, 1953, which I have read to the committee, set forth what I consider to be a very fair statement of government policy with respect to competition in civil aviation. I think it is a sound policy. In the last analysis the real test is what is going to be best for the Canadian people, what is going to be best for the aviation industry itself, and what in effect is going to produce the best over-all result.
Where in a particular region there is only a certain amount of money to be made, surely

It seems to me that is elementary; and it seems to me that the specific case to which I have just referred is an excellent example showing how undesirable it would have been-certainly in the fall of last year-to introduce competition in that particular region.
With those remarks I hope the committee will feel that the policy of the government in the matter of civil aviation is one which is designed to promote a healthy aviation industry, healthy finances for the carriers and good service for the people to be served.

Just a moment ago, in reply to the hon. member, I said I had not read the complete record at that time, that I merely considered a draft of the judgment and that the formal judgment I approved later was also all that I had read of the record up to that time. Mr. Chairman, I have already said that I had not read the record at the time; but as I conceive my duties under the Aeronautics Act, they are to assume responsibility for deciding whether as a matter of policy the decision of the air transport board ought to be confirmed or ought not to be confirmed. Mr. Chairman, did the same circumstances and the same reasons apply in connection with the application of the Liard River Air Service for a licence to operate a class 4, group "C"~ air service from Lower Post, British Columbia? If the hon. member believes those facts I think he has been misinformed. As far as I am concerned I had no other part in this particular appeal than that of confirming the decision of the board and ultimately considering the appeal that was taken from the board's decision. I made no suggestions to the board. I never had any occasion to discuss the matter with the board. If anything the hon. member has said implies that I did so, I must say to him that he has been misinformed on the subject.

May I ask the
minister whether representations were made to him or to any member of his department concerning either of these cases subsequent to the hearings by the air transport board and before the decisions of the air transport board were published, or if he knows whether any representations were made to the air transport board in person or otherwise between the time of the hearings and the time of the decisions?

So far as my departmental officials are concerned, my deputy minister tells me that he knows of no representations whatever having been made to the officials of my department. Carried.

Would the minister outline for us his interpretation of the actual status of the air transport board in connection with these hearings and decisions, from the standpoint of whether they constitute an independent' quasi-judicial body which is entitled to make decisions independent of interference by anyone other than the board personnel?
