I think, Mr. Chairman, it is perfectly clear from the statute that the air transport board has not only the authority but the responsibility of itself rendering decisions on the cases that are brought before it. I think under the act the minister has the responsibility of approving or disapproving those decisions. I think, as the hon. member knows, that the minister has the responsibility of disposing of any appeal that may be taken from a decision of the board. I did not write the statute. The statute is there and it is my duty to carry it out as it has been passed by parliament, and I have done my best to fulfil that duty.

Might I ask if it is the intention in the future that the minister or the government will be the deciding factor in determining the economics of any given situation in connection with applications of this kind; or shall the air transport board, within the bounds of the policy laid down by the previous minister of this department, have the authority to determine the complete economics of any given situation, not simply the geographic economics as outlined by the minister?

I think the hon. member should realize fully that the situation is covered by the statute, and the minister is not going to say anything which either goes beyond the statute or restricts its operation.

If I heard correctly a remark of the minister a few minutes ago, he said he could not possibly be expected to read in detail all the evidence brought forward at the various hearings of such bodies as the air transport board. I quite agree that is a very reasonable statement of his position. However, I think the minister would agree that the air transport board and other similar bodies deal with matters of important public policy that have a very direct effect upon the lives of citizens in various parts of Canada at different times.
In this connection I should like to mention that a hearing of the air transport board was held on the west coast last summer which was very much concerned with the matter of air transport in my constituency, and the decisions that were to be taken were a matter of great interest to a large number of people in that area. I took the trouble to go to Vancouver at the time the hearings were getting under way and sat in as an observer for one day. It was obvious to me that with the representations being made by the various legal counsel involved, the hearing was going to go on for quite a

Supply-Transport
number of days. I did not feel that my schedule warranted staying there for the full period.
However, being rather new to the functioning of such bodies, I wrote the secretary of the air transport board and asked if I could secure a copy of the evidence so I would be able to look it over at my leisure. I was informed I would have to write to the reporting organization which was reporting the proceedings. I thought it might perhaps cost me a little money, but I wrote and asked when the evidence would be available and how much it would cost me. If the reply had been that the cost would be $10, $15 or $25 I might have grumbled but I probably would have ordered it, but I was told that to get a complete copy-I cannot remember the exact figure-would cost me over $300.
I believe I sat down and wrote a letter to the minister, who had then recently assumed his office, about the matter. I raise the question now because while it is perfectly true the minister is not going to be able to go through all these things, it does seem to me nevertheless that, granting that these are matters of very great concern to many people in the country, there would be some advantage in members of the house being able to give a detailed perusal to reports of such hearings as may affect the particular areas from which they come. If there were any real reason to form an opinion that the board had not in fact arrived at a decision in the best public interest as far as the area was concerned, we would then be in a position to make proper representations to the minister and ask him to look into the specific question.
I should like the minister to indicate whether some consideration could not be given to a change in the present arrangements which would make that possible. I was informed, of course, that a copy of the transcript of such proceedings is available for the use of members in Ottawa, but if at the particular time we want to use it we happen to be three or four thousand miles away we have the choice in effect of paying $300 for a transcript of the evidence or of taking the time and going to the expense of making a trip to Ottawa. Neither of these alternatives may be particularly attractive at the time when we would like to be able to give a little serious study to the question of what sort of picture had been presented at the hearing and whether we, as representatives of the area, could feel completely satisfied with the decision arrived at by a body such as the air transport board.
[Mr. Barnett.}

Since the hon. member has referred to the air situation at Vancouver, I should like to ask the minister if the purchase or merger by Pacific Western Airlines of Queen Charlotte Airlines has been given approval by the air transport board. He might also inform us of the amount involved in connection with the transfer of one company to the other.

I understand that the matter has been approved in principle, but I cannot go further at the moment. I understand there is some urgency about the matter and that the board did render a decision just before the end of last month, I think. I have not a copy of the decision and I am not in a position to supply the information which the hon. member would seem to like to have. Quite frankly, I think I should also add that I am not certain just to what extent the figures are a matter of public knowledge or are the private concern of the parties.

I should like to speak shortly on this matter. I think the information at our disposal again discloses a situation which might require some investigation. It is my understanding that the purchase price being paid for this air line is considerably in excess of $1 million. At the same time I understand that the actual physical assets of the company are worth approximately $500,000. This presents, I think, two problems. First of all, the procedure in connection with the transfer of licences is very adequately set out in rule No. 3 of the air transport board dated October 16, 1952, which requires disclosure in full of practically every phase of the transfer of operations. I think by precedent the board has laid down the rule that no consideration shall be allowed for the transfer of air transport board licences.

If I might interrupt the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, my understanding of the matter is that the transaction which the board was asked to approve was not a transfer of assets but the acquisition of shares. I think the hon. member will admit that greatly affects the situation. We are not in a position, at the moment, to discuss the transfer of a licence. If the hon. member thinks he should say something about the transfer of shares, I think that would be quite in order. I feel the line he is pursuing has not much relation to the facts.

I think I can relate the remarks I am going to make to the transfer of shares because it presents this problem that, according to the company, a certain consideration must be paid for those shares. If, in fact, we follow the precedent

that no consideration should be allowed for the transfer of a licence or licences which will go along with the acquisition of the shares, then we find that in this case a considerable sum of money was paid for only one purpose, as I see it, and that is the actual acquisition of the operational rights of this air line.
If the consideration in transactions of this kind is going to be so much in excess of the physical values of the company it can have only one result, a result which I think the air board has heretofore tried to guard against, and that is the maintaining of a higher schedule of rates for the travelling public. No one is going to pay these top prices for assets of this kind without expecting an adequate return on his investment. In this particular case, if that kind of cushion is involved in the transaction then you can rest assured that the people in this area in British Columbia will pay the piper.
The second thing about this transaction that bothers me is that over the period of the last couple of years the air line which is being taken over has been helped to the extent of $200,000 or $250,000 in connection with its operations. If the cushion about which I have spoken is as large as I believe it is-and I think the facts will prove it-I can only come to one further conclusion, and that is that the owners of this air line are now putting into their own pocket approximately a quarter of a million dollars of the money of the people of Canada. Obviously the purchase price that is being paid would not be available to those owners if this substantial subsidy had not been paid over to them during the last couple of years.
I only suggest to the minister that if that type of assistance is required in the future there is only one answer, and that is that there should be some strings attached. The minister will recall that he replied to a question of mine several months ago in connection with a reported transaction of this kind, and he indicated to me there was no way of getting this money back.
Who did that?
You did.
Getting what money back?
The money that had been paid in subsidies to this company. 1 would leave him that one thought, that in future the people of Canada might be better protected in these transactions than they have been.

I am afraid I cannot leave these statements unchallenged. The hon. member started off on an assumption which I
Supply-Transport
find it difficult to accept, and that is that the price paid is substantially in excess of the value of the assets. I have no information which would enable me either to confirm or deny that assertion, because as I understand the matter no valuation has been made of the assets. Consequently I think it would be quite impossible to say whether the price being paid for these assets is too high or too low.
I note what the hon. member has said, and I think he ought perhaps to reflect on whether the position he is taking is that operators must be limited in the price they are to get for their investment to the book value of their assets and nothing more. If he would stop and think about it he would realize that the aviation industry generally would not be very anxious to accept that position.
Everybody else has up to this time. I do not believe in it myself, but that has been the case.

I do not know why, if the hon. member does not believe in it, he is affirming the contrary and saying that the price paid is too great. The hon. member then leaped to the conclusion that this price may be translated into higher rates. Since when has the price paid been the basis of rate making? Surely it is a cardinal principle of rate making that rates are made on the capital that is usefully invested in the enterprise, not on what was paid by the buyer to the seller in order to procure the seller's investment. That basis was discarded years ago.
So far as I am concerned I can see no reason at all why anybody should believe that because he pays a high price for something-and I am not expressing any opinion on the price-that necessarily justifies his getting rates afterwards to cover a price which was too high. All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that I think the board will be guided by the principle that it is the capital usefully invested in the enterprise that must be taken into account in the determination of rates.
The hon. member has criticized the fact that subsidies were paid for two years to one of these air lines. I do not think there was any question at all but that at the time these subsidies were paid it was necessary that they be paid in order to maintain the service the people in these communities had been getting. If the subsidies had not been paid the service would have been discontinued.
I think the hon. member understands the difference between a subsidy and a loan. If it were a loan it would be possible to demand

Supply-Transport
repayment. On the other hand, if a loan had been made to what extent would it have helped the company and to what extent would it have affected its subsequent credit? It is very easy to be wise after the event, and quite possibly the hon. member now would say that we should have thought of something else three or four years ago. All I can say is that I feel quite convinced that when the department and the government agreed to grant the subsidy two or three years ago it was because they felt that was the way the situation should be handled in the light of the circumstances.
The fact that the enterprise is now a useful going concern, which seems to have a value for others is, I believe, a vindication of the policy that was followed. It shows that an enterprise that seemed to be on the verge of financial difficulties has in consequence become an attractive property for someone else.

I think I should make one thing quite clear. As a matter of fact it has been the complaint of the industry that there has been too tight control over the ability of the owner to take advantage of the work he has put into his business when he is selling it. That seems to have been the complaint about the policy in the past. The objection I have raised here is to the fact that this sale price being paid does not reflect that type of consideration, but reflects a payment made by the government of this country.

I have two items upon which I should like to have the minister's comments. The first concerns information circular No. 0/5/55, which was issued last February 15, announcing the increase in storage rates for private aircraft. Those increased storage rates, I understand, became effective on April 1, and in some instances the amount was almost one and one-half times the previous rate. The reason I rise at this time is that I fail to understand the logic behind this increase in rates, in view of several circumstances that have prevailed hitherto.
In the first instance, many of the hangars operated by the Department of Transport which have been used by private aircraft operators in the storing of their aircraft were taken over from the Department of National Defence following the end of world war II. I would imagine that in these instances no tremendous cost of either original purchase or of upkeep would be involved. Then up to the present time the Department of Transport has operated a subsidized training program to encourage the acquisition of private licences by young Canadians who are

interested in flying. As I look in the estimates this year I notice an increase from $270,000 to $275,000 for this training.
Which item is that?

I am talking generally about item 433, and have made particular reference to the program of subsidized training which has increased last year's figure from $270,000 to $275,000. Unfortunately I cannot tell the minister under just which vote it is to be found, but it is-
To encourage private flying.

Yes, to encourage private flying. One reason I fail to understand the increased storage rate is that the increase, which is one and a half times the former rate, will tend to have a deterrent effect on the subsidized training program. In other words, the one measure seems to cancel out the other.
Would the minister give some indication of how many pilots have received their private licences under this subsidized program?
Would the hon. member hold his question until we reach the item dealing with that subject. If he wishes to talk about building rentals I shall be glad to answer him under this item, however.

I shall wait until we reach that specific item, but I mention it now just to prepare the minister so he may have an answer when the time comes. There might be a suggestion that there is to be a different approach to this subsidized training program, which would mean that the department would maintain closer control over the trainees, and there might be an attempt to co-ordinate the training program with the needs of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Of course that is sheer speculation. But the increase in storage rates, which in some cases will make it necessary for pilots trained under the subsidized program to dispose of their aircraft, would seem to indicate that there are two policies in conflict with each other.
Then there is another matter. In many of these hangars which have been made available as a result of being declared surplus following the war, large areas are allotted at relatively low rates for the storage of cars, trucks, farm machinery and that sort of thing. This would seem to be discriminatory against the owners of private aircraft, when they are asked to pay the exorbitant rates which would be necessary under the new schedule.
There are possible explanations for this situation. Special concessions are granted to

flying club operations, and that is as it should be. But unfortunately, particularly in the more remote parts of the country, where private flying operations are important to doctors and persons in other activities, there are no flying clubs organized to make it possible to come under the lower rates.
Then there is another possible explanation, one which has been discussed publicly in certain quarters. There might be a deliberate attempt on the part of the Department of Transport to eliminate some of the private aircraft. At least that suggestion has been put forward since recent air incidents, some of which have been tragic. It has been stated that it would be in the best interests of safer flying if there were fewer private operations.

I think I might tell the hon. member that he can cease speculating in that direction, because there has been no such intention on the part of the department or of the government. It is true that for aircraft belonging to flying clubs a nominal rental is charged; but individuals who have aircraft pay standard rates for the storage of those aircraft. Individuals who own aircraft must pay the storage charges for the space they occupy in departmental hangars. We have no intention of discriminating against them, but the fact is that it has been drawn to the attention of the department that the rates charged until recently for hangar space were not economical. They had not taken account of departmental costs for the services the people were getting. There has been no other thought in mind except to bring rentals more nearly in line with the costs of the service rendered.

I am glad to have the minister's reassurance in that regard. I would reiterate, however, that unfortunately it is going to disturb and discourage a certain amount of private flying, and particularly private ownership. I have had representations made to me in the matter as a result of the question I asked in the house last March. Also I have had representations from the Canadian owners' and pilots' association, which represents 1,500 private pilots and 700 aircraft owners. They have suggested, to get around this difficulty, that it might be possible to introduce a reduction to the extent of 50 per cent in the prevailing storage rate for all privately registered aircraft under 5,000 pounds.
As a concrete example of the situation which would prevail with an arrangement of this kind, they have given the following figures. Under the rate prevailing before the revision on April 1, the annual storage rate
Supply-Transport
would be $381.30. The new rate is $821.25 which, of course, cannot possibly be met by an individual. A 25 per cent reduction based upon a year's lease, or a proportionate share of a year's lease, would leave the figure at $615.94; and the suggested 50 per cent reduction would bring the storage rate for the year to $410.63. This puts the charge within the range of possibility of the ordinary private operator. The fact that the group most interested and most directly in contact with the operators, that is- the Canadian owners' and pilots' association, are so concerned over this matter should deserve the minister's attention.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to another matter which interests me.

I shall compress what I
have to say into a very few minutes. I think the question of safety of air travel is of great importance. Without going into too great detail, it was revealed by the evidence when the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines was before the committee that that air line is not responsible for the various methods of controlling the landing of aircraft, that in so far as the airports are concerned that is the responsibility of the Department of Transport. I was interested in the landing systems. I am speaking as a layman in regard to this, and as a passenger in aircraft. I have no technical

knowledge, but I was interested in the instrument landing system and in the ground control approach. Having memorized the meaning of those initials, I.L.S. and G.C.A., I notice that the minister has now thrown at us V.O.R.

same thing, but it is another one to learn about. My interest in this arose from a study of the report and the complete evidence with regard to the accident that occurred at Malton airport last fall, in the course of which the airplane was being operated on I.L.S. The question arises, would that accident perhaps not have happened had G.C.A. equipment been provided? In the course of questioning in committee on April 1, I asked the president of T.C.A. whether his organization had made any request to the transport board for the provision of G.C.A. equipment. I think it would be helpful if the minister would give us some indication as to the plans of the department with regard to this matter. I appreciate the fact that G.C.A. equipment is expensive. The safety record of T.C.A.-

Earlier I asked the chairman at which stage-

methods of controlling the landing of aircraft under difficult flying conditions, by means of I.L.S. or G.C.A. I think it is a matter of great public importance and I should like to have the minister's statement with regard to the policy of the department.

I shall try to give just a brief comment on this subject. I have suffered from the same difficulties of mastering the alphabet as those to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago. The last thing I want to do is try to create the impression that in a short time I have learned all about this very complex subject. But I am told that one of the principal reasons we have instrument landing systems at our major airports is that it was the preference of the civil aviation operators.
We have G.C.A. at Gander at the present time. The installation that was there when I was there in October is on a commercial basis. There is an installation which we are in process of completing, as I said yesterday. The difference between the two systems, as I understand it, is that the instrument landing system will function when the ceiling is not lower than 300 feet. In the case of G.C.A. I understand it will function even when the ceiling is as low as 100 feet. The fundamental difference, I believe, is that with the I.L.S. it is the pilot who decides what he should do in operating the aircraft, whereas with G.C.A. the pilot receives his directions from two operators on the ground. The hon. member would probably find it very interesting to see the operation carried out from the ground or in the aircraft, and I must admit that personally I was very much impressed when I saw the operation carried out at Gander last October.
The factor of expense is a very real one. My understanding is that a G.C.A. installation is worth between $800,000 and $1 million. When you have met the initial capital cost, you have to provide for the cost of the operators. When I was in Gander I was told that the unit there was being operated by two civilian employees of the air lines and that each received a salary in the neighbourhood of $10,000 a year. There were two men there, and I take it there would be probably two or three shifts. So my hon. friend will understand that G.C.A. not only is costly initially but is also costly to operate once it is installed. Conditions at Gander are different from those at the other major airports, and I think there is a good reason for having it there which does not hold for the other major airports.

I am interested in the cost factor, of course, but what is the cost factor

when an airplane has an accident and the people on board suffer injury or death? That has to be taken into consideration. It sounds rather alarming when you put the figure at $1 million for the installation of equipment and it is, of course, a heavy cost for operation; but that has to be balanced against the saving of lives as well as of aircraft.
I hope some means will be found of getting over that particular difficulty, because it is rather hard to estimate the value of a human life. Air traffic, as the minister will agree, is steadily increasing, and the problems of landing aircraft under difficult weather conditions will be even greater as time goes on, because flights are coming or going at all hours. Even on that occasion at Malton last fall there were aircraft landing before and after the one which suffered the accident. I hope the cost of installation will not prevent the minister from going ahead with plans for making it safer for air traffic.

Mr. Chairman, of course it is very easy to bring the factor of human life into these things. However, the fact remains that T.C.A. has not expressed a preference for G.C.A. at all the major airports. If my hon. friend will stop to think for a moment of the cost of equipping 10 or 15 major airports at approximately $1 million apiece, plus an operating cost of $100,000 a year for each installation, he may realize perhaps that it is easier when one is in opposition to suggest such large expenditures than it is when one has the responsibility of government.
I would suggest that if the the minister cut by one-third the cost of telephones and telegrams in his department-
Nonsense!
-he could put in G.C.A. equipment at one of these airports.

speechtext: We would rather hear you.

I should like to bring a
matter to the minister's attention that is of great consequence to the rural residents of my constituency. I have mentioned it on previous occasions. I refer to radio interference. I think I am on the right item. The interference is occasioned by the erection and installation of power lines in the district, particularly the power lines of the West Kootenay Power and Light Company, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and the British Columbia Power Commission. I realize these power lines are welcomed by the people and bring tremendous improvements, but they do create a problem, particularly in the rural sections of my riding, as far as radio reception is concerned because of the weak radio signals.
Last year when I brought up the matter in the house I suggested to the minister that I did not think it was quite good enough for his officials to say to these people that they could not do anything about it, while at the same time going after the little man with a small motor or something of that sort and making him comply with the law or pay a fine of $50. I know the matter does present great problems but I suggest that the minister's officials should get in touch with the companies concerned. They are reasonable people, and there should be some way of at least considerably lessening the interference as the result of co-operation between the minister's officials and the officials of the

companies concerned. The previous minister thought that was a good suggestion. He said he would have the matter investigated and have his officials visit the officials of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and the West Kootenay Power and Light Company.
I have not heard anything further about the matter, and I wonder whether the minis

ter has any idea what was the result of that investigation. I should also like to say that owing to the extension of the lines of the British Columbia Power Commission the same condition is now affecting the people along the Arrow lakes. I know there are great difficulties. It is not a simple problem, but I do think something could be achieved as the result of co-operation. Technical advice could be obtained, possibly advice as to some very inexpensive gadgets that would assist. I do not think it is sufficient to say "We are very sorry, but you will have to buy a better machine, a high priced machine." I bring the matter to the minister's attention because it is very irritating to people to have radio interference in the form of a constant roar for 24 hours a day.

I fully understand the feelings the hon. member has just expressed. I understand that something has been done since he spoke on the subject last year. However, I am told it is very difficult to eliminate interference completely in the neighbourhood of high power transmission lines. We receive a large number of complaints about interference, and I can say to the hon. member that with the staff available we do our best to investigate them and to dispose of the causes of interference where possible. If the hon. member would like to draw a specific area to my attention privately I would be very glad to make inquiries and to see what can be done.

Is any inspection made of power lines? I ask that question for this reason. I have had some experience with this kind of interference involving rural lines and I know there are two main causes for it. The first is, of course, a faulty transformer; the second, which is probably not so well known, arises when the ties used to tie the wires to the insulators are not tucked in tightly so that no ends are left sticking out. If there is an end even half an inch long that is not drawn up tightly around the high tension wire it will cause interference.
I think the hon. member is right.

Supply-Transport Meteorological division-
494. Administration, operation and maintenance, $7,374,500.

Last April the Canadian Press circulated a dispatch issued by the government's meteorological division under the heading, "Rainmakers Branded a Flop". This news dispatch dealt with the very interesting and worth-while experiment that has been going on in the semi-arid areas of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It is a voluntary effort supported in the main by some 2,700 farmers and covering over 3 million acres of land.
I believe the officials of the department under Dr. Thomson were asked to make an evaluation of the success of the experiments that have been going on since 1953, and apparently the results of that evaluation were summed up in the phrase, "Rainmakers Branded a Flop." I suggest that this is too hasty a summation of the sort of work that has been going on, because the individuals concerned do not agree at all with the findings of the department. Their opinion is that they have been successful in certain experimental areas in increasing precipitation by at least 25 per cent. I think the department's figures indicated a decline in precipitation in the experimental areas of some 14-1 per cent.
I am interested in this matter because I believe the experiment has not yet run its course, and there are other authorities not directly concerned with the experiments who agree with this viewpoint. Experiments are being conducted internationally in both the United States and Canada, and the President of the United States has recently set up an advisory committee on weather modification to go more fully into the results of similar efforts that are being carried on south of the border.
The whole project developed out of wartime research where it was discovered that under the right circumstances rain could be produced from clouds by artificial means, that is seeding the clouds with silver iodide. The people in the United States behind the project are quite creditable so far as their scientific qualifications are concerned. The weather research development corporation there, from which the Canadian effort springs, was founded by Dr. Irving Krick, who was on the allied weather team that gave the green light for the D-day invasion of Normandy. Dr. Krick later headed the meteorological department of the California Institute of Technology.
One of the specific criticisms of the departmental report was to the effect that the clouds had been overseeded. I am informed that such a situation, while it is possible

Supply-Transport
under laboratory conditions, is quite impossible in its practical application. Because of the air masses and the huge cloud formations involved, you could never have a situation of overseeding. I merely raise the point, Mr. Chairman, to suggest that it is too early to be as definite on this experiment as the report indicates. The fact, for example, that just a few days ago the operation centred in the city of Brandon was requested to fly 20 of their machines into Quebec is proof of the interest in the experiment. They landed at Dorval airport just a few days ago in the hope they might cause rainfall and thus assist in fighting the forest fires that are raging in the province. I hope that the heading, "Rainmakers Branded a Flop", is not actually the attitude of the department towards these people.

I had occasion to talk to Dr. Thomson on this subject several weeks ago. He showed me some very interesting graphs and figures in connection with the preliminary investigation that had been carried out by the department. I certainly formed the very clear impression from my conversation with him that what has appeared in the press is merely an outline of his report, and that the expression "flop" which was used by my hon. friend was not used by Dr. Thomson. I do not think for an instant it was intended to be implied that his conclusions were definite and final, and that the matter was closed.
In his conversation with me, at least, he said he had merely covered a period of years and I must say that the figures seemed to support the view he had expressed, that it has not proven its usefulness; but I do not believe he thought that was closing the door upon a further examination of the subject or that by making a report at this stage that was to be the end of the whole subject.
I understand that consideration of the subject and observations are to continue. I hope, for the sake of the people of the city of Brandon and the people they seem to have engaged from the United States, that it will be found these people are able to do something. Perhaps he might confer with the hon. member who spoke earlier on the desirability of doing these things in Canada.
The minister is under a misapprehension. It is a local group of farmers, 2,700 Canadian farmers, who have put up the necessary funds to carry on this experiment.
They hired the United States company.

They have the benefit of the research and background facilities of the

United States company, but it is entirely a Canadian operation. In Saskatchewan there are two co-operatives engaged in the same process, so that on the Canadian side it is entirely a Canadian effort.
Certainly there is the effort of paying, anyway.
I wonder if the minister has a long range forecast of the weather in Ottawa for the next month?
If the hon. member is asking my opinion about whether he should continue to ask questions on my estimates, I would say we were in for a prolonged hot spell.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to say to the minister that I was very pleased with the decision that was made by the appropriate officers of his department not long ago restoring his wings to Captain Norman Ramsay. I do not intend to go into the case any further. I said what I felt was necessary at the time I thought it was necessary, and I merely say, as I have already indicated, that I am very glad the decision to ground this pilot has been reversed and that he has the right to fly again.

I think that is not quite the situation, Mr. Chairman. I understand that Captain Ramsay has passed the necessary medical examination in order to be reinstated, and he now has to pass an instrument flight test before his licence is again available to him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am glad to have that correction.
I merely wanted to make the facts quite clear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would say the situation is hopeful. If he has passed the medical test and is being given permission to take the instrument landing test, I am sure Captain Ramsay will pass it without any question. The question I should like to put to the minister is this. Has there been any review by the appropriate officers of his department, or by the air transport board, of the regulations respecting flying, with particular reference to the cycle a pilot is permitted to fly? We all recognize that there are regulations that limit the number of hours per week, per month or per year that a pilot can fly,

but as we also know it is possible for a pilot to put in hours in a cycle that could be rather concentrated. I ask the minister the question as to whether there has been or will be any review of the length of the cycle that is permitted?

The whole question of the subject of pilot fatigue is, I think, under very active consideration not only in Canada but before the international civil air organization. I feel quite sure from what I have read in some periodicals that it is under consideration in the United States and elsewhere. I understand the subject is to be discussed in the fall, but in the meantime so far as we are concerned here in Canada my departmental officials who are concerned are giving very close study to the whole subject. It is not a matter which comes under the air transport board. It is a departmental matter and is dealt with by the department itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words it comes under this particular item?
Yes, I think so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And when the minister said the matter is to be discussed this fall, what did he mean?
At the ICAO meeting.
I think your arithmetic is wrong.
That is just an approximation.
It is too high.

The aircraft of the department are used primarily and principally for departmental purposes

verification of radio aids, transport of officers and officials in the field in connection with the carrying out of their duties at airports and, to a very small extent, in connection with the transport of ministers of the crown.
I should add that so far as my colleagues are concerned, they know the Department of Transport prefers that they use T.C.A. when flights are available. But flights are not always available at times when ministers of the crown have to leave on government business. Consequently the figures my hon. friend mentioned a moment ago indicating the number of flights that have taken place in which ministers of the crown have been transported in departmental aircraft represent, I think, a rather fair view of the situation. But it represents only a relatively small proportion of the number of flights of these aircraft.
I shall not hesitate to express the opinion that the use of aircraft for business purposes of this kind is likely to grow, because it is a great saver of time and it permits ministers and government officials and employees to accomplish their business more rapidly and more efficiently. I think-and I realize that this might not be a popular statement-that there is likely to be a growing use of departmental aircraft for these purposes, just as there is a growing use in industry of aircraft for executive officers. The

Supply-Transport
ministers do use T.C.A. and commercial air lines where such flights fit in with their schedules. But when the flights do not fit in, when it has the aircraft available the department will permit ministers to use its aircraft on government business.
I realize there is another question I have not touched upon, that of the Vickers Viscount. Someone-I would like to know who it was-suggested that the department had acquired a Vickers Viscount for the purpose of determining its airworthiness. Mr. Chairman, no serious-minded person would think for an instant that any department of government would spend public money for such purposes as that, and I hope no hon. member will give any credit to such an account.
The reasons were given in a certain amount of detail in reply to a question asked earlier in the session. I think the answer there given was complete. I might say that the pilots in my department, who have a great deal to say about the formulation of rules for travel in the air, have emphasized to me most forcefully how important it is that if they are to make these recommendations, they should have the experience of flying in high-speed jet aircraft. This does not mean that every time a new jet-propelled aircraft is produced we must rush out and buy one; we have no such policy in mind. But departmental pilots are most insistent that we should have aircraft of this type so they may advise the officials in charge of air regulations what changes should be made from time to time in order to keep up with modern flight conditions at high speeds and high altitudes. Unless you have the experience yourself, it is obvious you cannot make recommendations to others.
I would like to emphasize-and I say this without any critical thought in mind at all about T.C.A. or, in fact, any of the other commercial air lines-that this is the kind of advice that must be formulated entirely independently of the wishes of civil air operators, so we will have a completely objective view of the situation.

I wish to make only a brief observation for the information of the minister or possibly some of his officials. Recently when 1 was in Uranium City they brought to my attention the fact that the civilian band from 30 to 23-5 megacycles is not guarded most of the time. I think radio there is taken care of by Canadian army signals, and I understand that their equipment and personnel are inadequate to take care of it. It would not be a matter of too much importance, were it not for the fact that there is a good deal of civilian aviation in the Athabasca area, par-

ticularly around Uranium City and Beaver-lodge. Just to give an indication, there are three commercial air lines working out of there and an official of one of them told me that last year they had 15,000 take-offs and landings. In addition there are untold numbers of private craft in there at all times of the year, and possibly some notice could be taken of this.
I shall do so.
Has the Vickers Viscount been delivered to the department and, if so, is it in use?
It was delivered in March and is being used for the joint training of pilots of the department and of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and is still in possession of T.C.A.
Where do you find the pilots who operate these aircraft classified?
They would come under item 49V.
Could the minister tell us why an expenditure of $6,741 for travelling expenditures was made on behalf of Donald Bell, one of his employees?

I shall have to make inquiries. Perhaps I could furnish the information to my hon. friend.
